title: Physical regimes of quartic quantum advantage in elastic media simulation
summary: Quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation have been conjectured to offer up to a quartic quantum advantage over classical methods; however, the devil is always in the details. Here, we determine key physical conditions under which this quartic separation could be achieved in the relevant parameters. For continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with spatial convergence order $m$, we find that the end-to-end speedup is of order $(m+4)/(m+1)$ in the simulation time, and $4/(m+1)$ in the accuracy, with exponential memory advantage. For elastic lattice systems, we define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) as those that can be efficiently extracted from a quantum state, but cannot be resolved by a known continuum model with fewer degrees of freedom than the lattice. We then argue that the estimation of MRBOs is a candidate problem for quartic quantum advantage in problem size. We propose MRBOs for pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit end-to-end application where this occurs, while admitting efficient `quantum cheese' encodings of the material properties. We thus demonstrate how the interplay between regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity and quantum encodability constrains the relation between classical and quantum complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper pins down the physical conditions under which the conjectured quartic quantum advantage for elastic media simulation actually holds, showing end-to-end speedups of order (m+4)/(m+1) in simulation time and 4/(m+1) in accuracy for continuum systems, and proposing microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) in heterogeneous lattices as an explicit quartic-advantage application.
AI.motivation: Prior work conjectured up to a quartic quantum speedup for elastic media simulation, but the specific physical regimes and parameter settings enabling such separation were unspecified. The authors aim to identify the concrete physical conditions governing when this advantage is realizable end-to-end, rather than only as a complexity-theoretic abstraction.
AI.method: For continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with spatial convergence order m, they derive the achievable end-to-end speedup scaling in simulation time and accuracy, including memory scaling. For elastic lattice systems they define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) as quantities efficiently extractable from a quantum state but not resolvable by any known continuum model using fewer degrees of freedom than the lattice, and construct pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit instantiation, while adopting efficient "quantum cheese" encodings of material properties.
AI.result: Continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with convergence order m yields an end-to-end speedup of order (m+4)/(m+1) in simulation time and 4/(m+1) in accuracy, with exponential memory advantage. Estimation of MRBOs is argued to be a candidate problem exhibiting quartic quantum advantage in problem size, demonstrated concretely via pseudorandom heterogeneous materials.
AI.conclusion: The realized advantage is governed by the interplay among regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity, and quantum encodability, which jointly constrain the relation between classical and quantum complexity; the conjectured quartic advantage survives only under specific conditions and specific observable classes.

title: FNO-Based Inverse Co-Design of Semiconducting Quantum-Dot Devices
summary: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising building blocks for scalable spin-based quantum processors, however their operational properties depend on several fabrication and control parameters, such as lithographic gate layout and applied voltages. Existing device architectures have been refined through repeated fabrication and experimental testing, producing layouts that support reliable device operation. However, this process does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties. We address these challenges by presenting a differentiable inverse co-design framework for electrostatically defined quantum dots that jointly optimises gate voltages and the gate electrode layout. A semiclassical Thomas--Fermi electrostatic simulator provides reference data for a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate, which predicts the two-dimensional charge-density field. The desired spatial distribution of the confined charge defines the target quantum-dot geometry for inverse design. The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative $L^2$ test error of just 0.6\% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations. Relative to the CPU-based physics simulator, the FNO achieves a 17,000-fold speed-up on GPU for a single design, with further performance gains enabled by batched inference. When embedded in a gradient-based design loop with fabrication constraints, the FNO can produce both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions. The ability to engineer these distinct confinement configurations demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, providing a route towards designing devices with distinct qubit-relevant operating properties prior to fabrication.

AI.tldr: A differentiable inverse co-design framework for gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots jointly optimizes gate voltages and gate electrode layout, using a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate trained on Thomas–Fermi electrostatic simulations to enable millisecond-scale gradient-based inverse design of double-dot confinement geometries.
AI.motivation: Gate-defined quantum dots are promising for scalable spin-based quantum processors, but their properties depend sensitively on fabrication and control parameters (gate layout, voltages). Conventional device design relies on repeated fabrication and experimental testing, which refines layouts but does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties.
AI.method: The authors build a semiclassical Thomas–Fermi electrostatic simulator to generate reference data, train an FNO surrogate to predict the 2D charge-density field, and define the target quantum-dot geometry via the desired spatial charge distribution. The FNO surrogate is embedded in a gradient-based inverse design loop with fabrication constraints to jointly optimize gate voltages and gate electrode layout.
AI.result: The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative L2 test error of 0.6% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations, achieving a 17,000-fold GPU speed-up over the CPU physics simulator for a single design (with further gains from batched inference). In the design loop, it produces both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, enabling pre-fabrication engineering of distinct confinement configurations and providing a route toward designing devices with tailored, qubit-relevant operating properties.

title: All Bell inequalities with a quantum advantage in the minimal scenario are self-testing
summary: In the minimal Bell scenario, all extremal quantum correlations are known, but the Tsirelson inequalities that delimit the quantum set remain poorly understood. We study which correlations can maximize a given Tsirelson inequality, and conversely, which inequalities are maximized by a given correlation. We show that every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a single, extremal correlation, and thus self-tests the corresponding realization. This characterizes all self-tests based on linear Bell inequalities in this scenario. We also show that at most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation. We identify these as polygons for a family of correlations realized by qubit states of arbitrary entanglement. This allows us to deduce that the quantum set is not self-dual.

AI.tldr: In the minimal Bell scenario, every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a unique extremal correlation (hence self-tests it), and the quantum set is shown to be non-self-dual.
AI.motivation: Extremal quantum correlations in the minimal Bell scenario are fully known, but the Tsirelson inequalities defining the quantum set remain poorly understood. The paper aims to clarify the relationship between inequalities and the correlations that maximize them.
AI.method: Analyze the correspondence between Tsirelson inequalities and extremal correlations: determine which correlations maximize a given inequality and conversely which inequalities a given correlation maximizes; characterize the families of inequalities maximized by nonlocal extremal correlations and identify their geometric structure.
AI.result: Every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a single extremal correlation, providing a complete characterization of linear-Bell-inequality-based self-tests. At most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation, identified as polygons for a family of correlations realized by qubit states of arbitrary entanglement. This implies the quantum set is not self-dual.
AI.conclusion: Linear Bell inequalities in the minimal scenario fully characterize self-tests, and the non-self-duality of the quantum set reveals a structural asymmetry relevant to understanding the quantum boundary.

title: Nonequilibrium Spin-Glass Order in a Long-Range Quantum Ising Glass and Its Sensitivity to Noise
comment: 27 pages, 23 figures: Letter (4 pages + End Matter, 3 figures) and Supplemental Material (20 figures)
summary: We study spin-glass order after a transverse-field quench in a long-range quantum Ising glass. The diagonal-ensemble Edwards-Anderson order coincides at the no-quench and zero-field endpoints, yet in between cold shells overshoot it and hot shells undershoot it. This stems from a competition in correlation space between the rigidity of populated eigenstates and the spread of their pair patterns. Under weak longitudinal dephasing the zero-field endpoint is exactly pinned while the characteristic finite-quench response fades, giving a self-referenced noise probe for quantum spin simulators.

AI.tldr: We analyze spin-glass order after a transverse-field quench in a long-range quantum Ising glass, showing that cold and hot shells overshoot and undershoot the endpoint Edwards-Anderson order due to competition between eigenstate rigidity and pair-pattern spread in correlation space.
AI.motivation: The Edwards-Anderson order parameter of a long-range quantum Ising glass is studied through its behavior after a transverse-field quench.
AI.method: A long-range quantum Ising glass is quenched in the transverse field. The diagonal-ensemble Edwards-Anderson order parameter is evaluated at the no-quench and zero-field endpoints and as a function of shell temperature. The effect of weak longitudinal dephasing is also analyzed.
AI.result: The diagonal-ensemble Edwards-Anderson order matches the no-quench and zero-field endpoint values, but intermediate shells deviate: cold shells overshoot, and hot shells undershoot. This originates from competition between the rigidity of populated eigenstates and the spread of their pair patterns in correlation space. Under weak longitudinal dephasing, the zero-field endpoint value is exactly pinned while the characteristic finite-quench response fades.
AI.conclusion: The behavior of the quench response provides a self-referenced noise probe for quantum spin simulators, as the pinned zero-field endpoint under dephasing yields a calibrated reference for the characteristic finite-quench response.

title: Nonlocal magic of fermions is bounded by entanglement fluctuations and is logarithmic for free fermions
summary: Free-fermion states are classically simulable, yet, written as qubits, they typically carry extensive magic, the quantum resource that stabilizer circuits lack. Part of this magic is nonlocal: local unitaries acting separately on two parts of the system cannot remove it. If these local unitaries are restricted to Gaussian ones, the nonlocal magic grows linearly with the number $m$ of partially entangled fermion pairs. We show that this growth is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction: local Gaussian unitaries minimize the nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy for up to three pairs, but not from four pairs on. General local non-Gaussian unitaries that respect fermion parity take $m$ free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with a fidelity that decays at most as $1/\sqrt m$ compared to exponential decay with Gaussian unitaries, so the nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in $m$. The reason is statistical --- Bell pairs have equal Schmidt weights, that is, a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum, and a state can stay far from them only if its Schmidt weights are spread over many orders of magnitude. This spread is measured by the capacity of entanglement $C_E$, the variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian, and the nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically with $C_E$. Free-fermion pairs add to $C_E$ independently, so $C_E$ grows only linearly in $m$, and this leads to the stabilizer fidelity decreasing at most as $1/\sqrt m$. Almost all the magic of free fermions, including Hartree--Fock and BCS mean-field states, is therefore local.

AI.tldr: Almost all of the extensive magic carried by free-fermion states is local; restricting to Gaussian local unitaries artificially makes nonlocal magic grow linearly, whereas general parity-preserving non-Gaussian unitaries reduce it to a logarithmic growth, bounded by the capacity of entanglement.
AI.motivation: Free-fermion states, while classically simulable, carry extensive magic when expressed in qubits, and part of this magic is nonlocal (not removable by local unitaries). The authors question whether the previously reported linear-in-m growth of nonlocal magic under local Gaussian unitaries is intrinsic or merely an artifact of the Gaussian restriction, and they seek the physical quantity controlling nonlocal magic.
AI.method: The authors study the nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy of free-fermion states (m partially entangled fermion pairs) under local Gaussian versus general fermion-parity-preserving non-Gaussian unitaries. They relate the minimum nonlocal magic to the fidelity with fermionic Bell pairs, and analyze the entanglement spectrum, introducing the capacity of entanglement C_E (variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian) as the key statistical measure. They show nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically in C_E, and since free-fermion pairs add to C_E independently, C_E scales only linearly in m.
AI.result: Local Gaussian unitaries minimize nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy only up to three pairs, failing from four pairs onward. General local non-Gaussian parity-preserving unitaries map m free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with fidelity decaying at most as 1/sqrt(m) (versus exponential decay for Gaussian unitaries), because Bell pairs have a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum and a state can remain far from them only if Schmidt weights spread over many orders of magnitude, as quantified by C_E. Consequently nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in m.
AI.conclusion: The linear growth of nonlocal magic under Gaussian local unitaries is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction. The capacity of entanglement bounds nonlocal magic logarithmically, and since free-fermion pairs contribute to C_E only additively, almost all the magic of free-fermion systems—including Hartree–Fock and BCS mean-field states—is local rather than nonlocal.

title: On the critical value of void percolation in high dimensions
summary: In the random Lorentz gas, a point tracer moves through spherical obstacles of (reduced) density $Φ$ centered on a Poisson point process in $d$-dimensional space, $\mathbb{R}^d$, and becomes localized once the vacant space stops percolating, at $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$. The dimensional scaling of this void percolation threshold has remained elusive. Prior bounds, conjectural ones included, ranged from $Ω(1)$ to $O(d\ln d)$, leaving even the scaling undetermined. We here prove that $Φ_{\rm p}(d)=Θ(d)$, and in particular that $\tfrac12\,d \le Φ_{\rm p}(d) \le 5\,d$ for all sufficiently large $d$. The upper bound counts hierarchical families of escape waypoints called tree embeddings; the lower bound is via a weighted second-moment estimate on an explicit ensemble of ballistic escape routes. A linear scaling of $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$ excludes the $d\ln d$ growth suggested by analogy with other systems in the random first-order transition universality class and is consistent with the numerical estimate $Φ_{\rm p}/d \to 3.40(5)$. Because the mean-field dynamical transition is likewise linear, $Φ_{\rm d}\simeq 2.40\,d$, our result fixes the activated window $[Φ_{\rm d},Φ_{\rm p}]$ as a bounded---rather than diverging---correction to mean-field dynamical arrest in sufficiently high $d$.

AI.tldr: The void percolation threshold of the random Lorentz gas in high dimension is proven to scale linearly: $\tfrac12 d \le \Phi_p(d) \le 5d$, settling a previously undetermined scaling.
AI.motivation: The dimensional scaling of the void percolation threshold $\Phi_p(d)$, at which the vacant space of the random Lorentz gas stops percolating, had remained unresolved. Prior bounds (including conjectural ones) spanned $\Omega(1)$ to $O(d\ln d)$, so even the leading-order scaling was unknown.
AI.method: Upper bound: counting hierarchical families of escape waypoints termed tree embeddings. Lower bound: a weighted second-moment estimate on an explicitly constructed ensemble of ballistic escape routes.
AI.result: $\Phi_p(d)=\Theta(d)$, specifically $\tfrac12 d \le \Phi_p(d) \le 5d$ for all sufficiently large $d$.
AI.conclusion: Linear scaling rules out the $d\ln d$ growth suggested by analogy with other random first-order transition systems and agrees with the numerical estimate $\Phi_p/d \to 3.40(5)$. Since the mean-field dynamical transition is also linear ($\Phi_d \simeq 2.40d$), the activated window $[\Phi_d,\Phi_p]$ is a bounded rather than diverging correction to mean-field dynamical arrest.

title: Threshold-Free Symmetry-Enriched Topological Quantum Memory
summary: We show that non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect a toric code memory against incoherent electric noise at any bond error probability $p\in[0,1]$. For a toric code on the honeycomb lattice coupled to $Sp(N)$ rotors, with electric anyons carrying the fundamental representation, we construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder whose logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for $N\ge40$, a conservative sufficient bound. The same decoder also rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of $Sp(N)$ under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions. The construction extends to other symmetries, including $SU(N)$.

AI.tldr: Non-Abelian symmetry enrichment lets a honeycomb-lattice toric code coupled to Sp(N) rotors suppress incoherent electric noise for all bond error probabilities, with an efficient minimum-weight decoder and exponential logical-error decay for N≥40.
AI.motivation: Standard toric-code memories fail above a threshold error probability; the authors ask whether non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect the memory at any bond error probability, and whether this connects to strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking under local decoherence.
AI.method: Couple a toric code on the honeycomb lattice to Sp(N) rotors with electric anyons in the fundamental representation; construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder and analyze its logical error probability as a function of system size and N; extend the construction to other symmetries such as SU(N).
AI.result: Logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for N≥40 (a conservative sufficient bound) at any p∈[0,1]; the same decoder rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of Sp(N) under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Non-Abelian symmetry enrichment provides full-range noise protection for toric code memories, yields a no-go for strong-to-weak SSB in the fundamental channel, and generalizes to other non-Abelian symmetries including SU(N).

title: Thermodynamics of Forgetting in a Bounded Hopfield Network
summary: A memory that keeps learning must also forget. The Hopfield network does not: beyond a critical number of stored patterns it falls into a state of total confusion and retrieves none of them. Parisi showed in 1986 that bounding the synaptic strength cures this pathology, since the clipping of the couplings gradually erases the oldest memories and leaves room for the new ones. In this paper we provide a thermodynamic description of the resulting network, known as the Hopfield-Parisi model. Starting from the learning rule, we show that the network is equivalent to a Hopfield model whose patterns are weighted according to their age, superimposed on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, both governed by the synaptic bound: a larger bound makes the memory longer, but also noisier. The theory of nonlinear networks developed in the eighties already provides, through the heuristic replica method, the equations that govern this model at any temperature, but to the best of our knowledge they have been solved only at zero temperature. We rederive them at the replica symmetric level through Guerra's interpolation and solve them at finite temperature, obtaining the phase diagram of the model together with its memory horizon, namely the largest age at which a pattern can still be retrieved. The solution shows that forgetting acts on the signal alone, the noise being the same for patterns of every age, and that the horizon is maximal at an intermediate bound which is essentially insensitive to temperature. Monte Carlo simulations of networks trained with the original learning rule support these predictions.

AI.tldr: The authors give a finite-temperature thermodynamic (replica-symmetric) solution of the Hopfield-Parisi model of bounded synapses, deriving its phase diagram and memory horizon and confirming them by Monte Carlo simulation.
AI.motivation: A learning memory must forget: the standard Hopfield network catastrophically fails beyond a critical load, retrieving none of its patterns. Parisi (1986) showed that clipping the synaptic strength cures this pathology by gradually erasing oldest memories. The resulting Hopfield-Parisi model lacked a full thermodynamic treatment; prior replica equations had only been solved at zero temperature.
AI.method: Starting from the learning rule, the network is mapped onto a Hopfield model with age-weighted patterns superimposed on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, both controlled by the synaptic bound. The governing equations are rederived at the replica-symmetric level via Guerra's interpolation and solved at finite temperature to obtain the phase diagram and memory horizon.
AI.result: Finite-temperature phase diagram and memory horizon are obtained. Forgetting acts on the signal alone (noise is age-independent), and the horizon is maximal at an intermediate synaptic bound that is essentially temperature-insensitive. Monte Carlo simulations of networks trained with the original learning rule support the predictions.
AI.conclusion: Bounded synapses yield a controlled trade-off between memory lifetime and noise: a larger bound prolongs memory but increases noise, with an optimal intermediate bound. The replica-symmetric finite-temperature solution quantitatively describes the Hopfield-Parisi model and matches simulations.

title: Single-shot ground-state preparation via strongly coupled baths
summary: Preparing ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems is a central task in quantum simulation. Dissipative protocols have emerged as a promising solution for both near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling, leading to slow cooling. Here, we construct cooling protocols at strong system-bath coupling, and demonstrate accurate state preparation within even a single cooling cycle. Our protocols combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, we reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem: ground-state cooling becomes a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. We then construct a family of ``Möbius-Ingham'' protocols, which reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra, as a function of the cycle period. In our free-fermion benchmarks, Möbius-Ingham cooling lies on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the controls tested. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in interacting Ising and $t$-$V$ chains and the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we extend our construction to Gibbs state preparation, showing how free-fermion thermal states can be prepared in a single cycle.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs strong-coupling dissipative cooling protocols—"Möbius-Ingham" controls—that prepare ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems accurately within a single cooling cycle, achieving optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and near-exponential suppression of heating for gapped spectra.
AI.motivation: Preparing ground and thermal states is central to quantum simulation, and dissipative protocols are promising for near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most existing constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling and thus cool slowly. The authors aim to overcome this slow-cooling limitation by operating at strong system-bath coupling.
AI.method: They combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, they reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem, recasting ground-state cooling as a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. They then construct a family of "Möbius-Ingham" protocols and validate them on free-fermion benchmarks, interacting Ising and t-V chains, the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model, and extend the construction to Gibbs state preparation.
AI.result: The Möbius-Ingham protocols reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra as a function of cycle period. In free-fermion benchmarks they lie on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the tested controls. The effectiveness is further demonstrated in interacting Ising and t-V chains and the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model, and free-fermion thermal (Gibbs) states can be prepared in a single cycle.
AI.conclusion: Strong-coupling dissipative cooling with time-dependent ramped ancilla levels and couplings enables accurate single-cycle ground-state preparation, with Möbius-Ingham controls offering favorable error-time trade-offs, and the approach generalizes to Gibbs state preparation.

title: Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
summary: Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.

AI.tldr: A disorder-agnostic ("blind") initial-state preparation, built only from the clean chain geometry and particle number, can still produce a strong-Mpemba-effect speedup in dephased disordered XX chains. At strong dephasing the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, where an exact inverse-generator identity links residual slow-mode overlap to the spatial resistance profile, yielding two distinct thresholds: finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the overlap decays as L^{-1/2} only if resistance variance is finite.
AI.motivation: Strong-Mpemba-effect relaxation speedup via initial-state design normally requires suppressing the slowest mode, which demands prior knowledge of the system. In disordered systems that mode is sample-dependent, so any fixed preparation typically retains a slow-mode overlap. The paper asks whether a preparation designed without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution can nonetheless yield a typical-sample speedup.
AI.method: Define a "blind" preparation from the clean chain, requiring only chain geometry and particle number. Study a dephased disordered XX chain and, in the strong-dephasing limit, map the density dynamics to a resistor chain. Use an exact inverse-generator identity to relate the residual slow-mode overlap to the spatial resistance profile, and perform finite-size calculations including interactions at strong dephasing.
AI.result: The blind preparation starts farther from stationarity yet overtakes a reference in typical samples. Two thresholds emerge: finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, whereas the residual overlap decays as L^{-1/2} with chain length L only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. The fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins is predicted as an ensemble-level reliability measure. Finite-size calculations confirm both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing.
AI.conclusion: Disorder-agnostic, geometry-only state preparation can deliver a typical-sample strong-Mpemba acceleration in disordered dephased chains, with reliability quantified by a predicted win-fraction. The work provides preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap, linking slow-mode suppression to the resistance profile's mean and variance.

title: Ground-State Dressing and Delayed Feedback of a Chiral Giant Atom in Ultrastrong Waveguide QED
summary: We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase π/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Using a variational polaron transformation, we show that the renormalized transition frequency and the total ground-state dressing inherit this independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. A sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. We also derive the spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, showing that, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the memory kernel becomes distance independent at the same phase.

AI.tldr: A chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a 1D waveguide at two separated points is studied; at a relative coupling phase of π/2 the total spectral density and renormalized ground-state properties become independent of the inter-point distance while the virtual-photon dressing stays chiral.
AI.motivation: Giant atoms with multiple spatially separated coupling points exhibit interference effects that depend on distance and coupling phases; the ultrastrong-coupling regime introduces counter-rotating terms and ground-state dressing, whose interplay with chirality and coupling-point separation is not well understood. The paper aims to clarify how a relative coupling phase can decouple bulk spectral properties from geometry while preserving directional (chiral) behavior.
AI.method: A chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. A variational polaron transformation is used to obtain renormalized transition frequency, ground-state dressing, and spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, including a memory kernel; the local photonic potential is neglected in the emission analysis. A sudden switch-off of the coupling is employed to release the virtual-photon cloud as directional radiation.
AI.result: At a relative coupling phase π/2, the total spectral density is independent of the coupling-point distance, whereas its directional components are not. The renormalized transition frequency and total ground-state dressing inherit this distance independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. Sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. In the polaron frame, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the spontaneous-emission memory kernel also becomes distance independent at the same phase.
AI.conclusion: A relative coupling phase of π/2 acts as a decoupling condition: total spectral and renormalized ground-state quantities become insensitive to the separation of the two coupling points, yet chirality persists in the directional components and virtual-photon cloud. This yields distance-robust, directionally emitting ultrastrongly coupled giant-atom dynamics relevant to chiral quantum photonics.

title: Quantum Noise Engineering in Advanced LIGO
comment: Submitted to Contemporary Physics. Open source tools developed for this manuscript can be found in: https://github.com/BKabagoz/LIGO-quantum-tools
summary: Advanced LIGO is a gravitational-wave detector with extreme sensitivity, operating close to the quantum limits of optical measurement. The quantum noise in this system arises from vacuum fluctuations entering the interferometer readout port: phase-like fluctuations produce measurement imprecision, while amplitude-like fluctuations drive radiation-pressure back-action. In this review, we present an intuitive description in terms of complex fields and quadratures, and follow squeezed vacuum from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity and propagation through the interferometer, to the readout. We discuss how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer quantum noise, and how correlations between optical quadratures map onto correlations between measurement imprecision and back-action. We conclude that LIGO is both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.

AI.tldr: A review of quantum noise in Advanced LIGO, described intuitively via complex fields and quadratures, tracing squeezed vacuum from generation through a filter cavity and interferometer to readout, and showing how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer imprecision and back-action correlations.
AI.motivation: Advanced LIGO operates near quantum limits of optical measurement, where vacuum fluctuations entering the readout port produce measurement imprecision (phase-like) and radiation-pressure back-action (amplitude-like). A clear conceptual account of these effects and of squeezing-based mitigation is needed.
AI.method: An intuitive quadrature/complex-field description: squeezed vacuum is followed from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity, and through propagation in the interferometer to the readout. Frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing are analyzed in terms of optical quadrature correlations mapping onto imprecision–back-action correlations.
AI.result: Frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing are shown to engineer quantum noise by reshaping correlations between optical quadratures and hence between measurement imprecision and back-action.
AI.conclusion: LIGO serves both as a gravitational-wave observatory and as a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.

title: Particle-loss error correction using $2^l$-step states generated via particle-number-resolving measurement schemes
summary: We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by $2^l$ ($2^l$-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. Our results identify the most efficient encoding, which achieves a higher channel fidelity than previously studied bosonic encodings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an iterative scheme to generate finite superpositions of Fock states with photon numbers separated by 2^l, gives an upper bound on their generation probability, and uses such states to build bosonic encodings for particle-loss error correction, identifying the most efficient encoding with improved channel fidelity over prior bosonic codes.
AI.motivation: Existing bosonic encodings for particle-loss correction are limited in channel fidelity; the authors seek better codes by exploiting a class of Fock-state superpositions with 2^l-spaced photon numbers, which may offer favorable loss-correcting structure.
AI.method: An iterative procedure is introduced to construct finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by 2^l (2^l-step states); the maximum achievable generation probability is upper-bounded analytically. Several bosonic encodings are then built from this state class and benchmarked on particle-loss error correction via channel fidelity comparisons.
AI.result: An upper bound on the probability of generating 2^l-step states is derived. Among the constructed bosonic encodings, one is identified as most efficient, attaining higher channel fidelity under particle-loss errors than previously studied bosonic encodings.
AI.conclusion: 2^l-step Fock-state superpositions provide a viable resource for loss-correcting bosonic codes, and the best encoding in this family outperforms earlier bosonic encodings in channel fidelity, though generation is constrained by the derived probability bound.

title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
summary: Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp$ reaches $10^8$ to $10^{10}$. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by $\|r_0\|_{L^+}(χ_\parallel-χ_\perp)^{-1/2}$, where the numerator does not depend on $χ_\parallel$. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as $χ_\parallel^{-1/2}$, which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp=10^9$, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives $1.3\times10^{-5}$. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of $7.0\times10^{-6}$ with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to $1.2\times10^4$ shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.

AI.tldr: Sample-based quantum subspace methods for strongly anisotropic heat conduction in magnetized plasmas are analyzed; aligning the measurement basis with flux surfaces yields bounds and errors that improve with anisotropy, whereas the computational basis suffers an error floor, confirmed on superconducting and trapped-ion hardware.
AI.motivation: Sample-based quantum subspace methods build a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. Applying these to heat conduction in magnetized plasmas is challenging because the parallel-perpendicular anisotropy χ∥/χ⊥ reaches 10^8 to 10^10, and it is unclear how the choice of measurement basis affects the achievable accuracy of the energy-norm Galerkin solution.
AI.method: The authors prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. (1) If the measurement basis is aligned with flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by ||r0||_{L+}(χ∥−χ⊥)^{−1/2}, with a numerator independent of χ∥; the bound is sharp. (2) In the computational basis, a subspace missing a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as χ∥^{−1/2}, producing an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. The aligned basis requires no time evolution: only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register. Validation uses a shaped cross-section and a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits, plus runs on a ten-qubit superconducting processor (768 shots) and a trapped-ion processor, and comparison with sample-based quantum diagonalization.
AI.result: Both results are verified numerically and on hardware. At χ∥/χ⊥=10^9, the computational basis yields an error of order unity regardless of shot budget, while a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives 1.3×10^5 error. On the ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis achieves a median error of 7.0×10^6 with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to 1.2×10^4 shots. The trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior, and the same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization.
AI.conclusion: Measurement-basis alignment with flux surfaces is essential for sample-based quantum subspace methods under extreme anisotropy: it gives provably sharp, anisotropy-improving error bounds with shallow circuits (state preparation plus a five-qubit QFT) and dramatically outperforms the computational basis on real quantum hardware, where the computational basis cannot overcome its error floor merely by increasing shots.

title: Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. In the proceedings of QCE 2026
summary: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.

AI.tldr: Dithered belief-propagation (BP) decoding is proposed for circuit-level quantum memory, combining a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation to suppress BP oscillations and trapping, achieving accuracy comparable to or better than Relay-BP with far cheaper arithmetic.
AI.motivation: Standard BP decoders for qLDPC codes suffer from oscillations and trapping behavior that degrade decoding performance, and existing remedies (e.g., BP+OSD, Relay-BP) are costly. The paper aims to mitigate these pathologies while remaining suitable for real-time quantum memory decoding.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dithered BP decoder that couples a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation, evaluated under circuit-level noise on a distance-11 rotated surface code and a distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, benchmarked against BP, BP+OSD+CS-10, and Relay-BP.
AI.result: The dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10 and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates. It incurs a moderate increase in additions but roughly 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminates node-level RNGs.
AI.conclusion: Dithering is a promising, computationally efficient direction toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.

title: Improving Gravitationally Induced Entanglement in Interferometric Configurations
summary: Proposals to detect gravitationally induced entanglement between massive particles offer a promising pathway toward probing the quantum nature of gravity. We perform a systematic geometric optimization and comparative analysis of Stern--Gerlach (SG) and Mach--Zehnder (MZ) matter-wave interferometers for this purpose, deriving exact analytical expressions for the gravitational phase of each configuration. Our first key result is that geometric optimization is indispensable. For commonly assumed experimental parameters, neglecting the optimization of geometric ratios can suppress the accumulated phase, and hence the detectability of entanglement, by up to several orders of magnitude. Second, we provide a complete comparative analysis of two SG orientations (linear and parallel) and three MZ orientations (translation-symmetric, mirror-symmetric, and parallel-arms). The parallel-arms SG and MZ configurations tend to yield the largest phase accumulations and are nearly equivalent in performance, whereas the translation-symmetric MZ setup exhibits destructive-interference nulls that act as blind operating points where detection becomes ineffective. These observations highlight the importance of geometry-aware design. A Monte Carlo error analysis of realistic fabrication tolerances indicates that the parallel-arms configurations are generally more robust, maintaining low relative phase uncertainty over broad parameter intervals. Furthermore, an evaluation of Bell violations assesses the feasibility and signal-to-noise ratio of each configuration. Our results identify geometric optimization, particularly through parallel-arms designs, as an important consideration for near-term experiments targeting gravitationally induced entanglement.

AI.tldr: Geometric optimization of SG and MZ matter-wave interferometers is essential for detecting gravitationally induced entanglement; parallel-arms designs maximize phase and are most robust under fabrication tolerances.
AI.motivation: Detecting gravitationally induced entanglement between massive particles is a promising route to probing the quantum nature of gravity, but the achievable gravitational phase depends strongly on interferometer geometry, which has not been systematically optimized or compared across configurations.
AI.method: Exact analytical expressions for the gravitational phase are derived for Stern–Gerlach (SG) and Mach–Zehnder (MZ) matter-wave interferometers, followed by geometric optimization of ratio parameters. Two SG orientations (linear, parallel) and three MZ orientations (translation-symmetric, mirror-symmetric, parallel-arms) are compared, with Monte Carlo error analysis of realistic fabrication tolerances and an assessment of Bell violations and signal-to-noise ratio.
AI.result: Neglecting geometric optimization can suppress the accumulated phase—and thus entanglement detectability—by up to several orders of magnitude. Parallel-arms SG and MZ configurations yield the largest phase accumulations and are nearly equivalent in performance; translation-symmetric MZ exhibits destructive-interference nulls acting as blind operating points. Monte Carlo analysis shows parallel-arms configurations are more robust, sustaining low relative phase uncertainty over broad parameter ranges.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware design, particularly via parallel-arms interferometer configurations, is a key consideration for near-term experiments targeting gravitationally induced entanglement, offering maximal phase accumulation and improved robustness to fabrication tolerances.

title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
summary: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable distributed quantum computing (DQC) transpilation method that couples a quantum interaction graph (QIG) graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic, achieving large cost reductions and speed-ups on restricted-connectivity superconducting DQC architectures at scale.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computing is a promising path to scale superconducting hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a transpilation bottleneck. Existing DQC transpilers assume idealized connectivity, ignore intra-module routing, or incur heavy computational overhead that limits scalability.
AI.method: A QIG-based graph-partitioning mapping step combined with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic, jointly designed to handle the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting architectures through coupled inter-module mapping and intra-module routing.
AI.result: On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs × 16 qubits) all-to-all inter-core architecture: up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured) reduction in average aggregated cost, with >250× speed-ups over DMapS for structured workloads. On 399-qubit (3×133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, the method keeps practical runtimes. Versus a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, structured routing costs drop by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core) and 51.96% (restricted line topology).
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a practical, scalable transpilation method for distributed quantum computing, outperforming state-of-the-art DMapS and DQC-adapted SABRE in both cost and runtime at scale.

title: Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
summary: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a thermal reservoir-computing paradigm where data is encoded in the time-dependent temperature of a heat bath, proving a rigorous structural memory–nonlinearity trade-off and showing via driven-qubit examples that large Hilbert spaces do not guarantee computational power.
AI.motivation: Heat generation is usually viewed as a limiting factor for computation, but in reservoir computing dissipation (fading memory) can be a resource. The authors seek to exploit thermal dissipation natively by encoding input data on the bath temperature, aiming for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.
AI.method: Data injection is encoded in a time-dependent bath temperature driving the reservoir. The authors derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout and prove a rigorous memory–nonlinearity trade-off, arguing it is a structural necessity since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. They illustrate with a single driven qubit (one free parameter) and with a pair of coupled qubits where breaking a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable.
AI.result: The trade-off is shown to be structural rather than a tunable dynamical regime. For the coupled-qubit system, the single observable accesses just over half of the fifteen-dimensional space despite symmetry breaking, refuting the assumption that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power.
AI.conclusion: The memory–nonlinearity trade-off is relocated from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, so observable choice and bath engineering (rather than Hamiltonian control) are identified as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

title: Upper and lower bounds for few-copy Gaussian tomography, and the absence of a fermionic warm regime
comment: 32 pages, 2 tables. Extends arXiv:2609.23189 to measurements on blocks of k copies; uses Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.26705 as a black box
summary: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$. The author proved $Ω(m^3/ε^2)$ for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of $k$ copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls $β\|h\|_F\leβ_0$ of unknown Hamiltonian $h$, the single-copy rate is $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ for every fixed $β_0>0$, at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of $β_0$. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives $N>m^3/(8{,}553{,}600\,k\,ε^2)$ for blocks of at most $k$ copies and all $ε\le1/3600$; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of $\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, shows that the budget $mt^2$ behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether $1/k$ is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need $Ω(m^3/(ε^2\min\{\sqrt k,m\}))$ copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the $k$-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every $k$ on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. This closes their $k$-entangled gap on the cold class; intermediate temperatures remain open.

AI.tldr: This note shows that the cold/warm crossover in bosonic Gaussian tomography has no fermionic counterpart: on quadratic Gibbs balls the single-copy rate is Θ(m³/ε²) for all fixed inverse temperatures, with lower-bound constants independent of β₀, and extends the fermionic bound to k-copy blocks (Ω(m³/(ε²·min{√k,m}))).
AI.motivation: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill established a bosonic crossover (cold states: Θ(m³/ε²); warm: Θ(m²/ε²)), and the author previously proved Ω(m³/ε²) for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. The motivation is to determine whether this cold/warm crossover persists for fermions and to generalize the single-copy lower bound to multi-copy (block) measurements.
AI.method: Fermionic Gaussian state tomography on quadratic Gibbs balls β‖h‖_F ≤ β₀; a replicated-parameter Fisher-information budget at the maximally mixed state; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information via spinor tensor powers of so(2m); an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography (with parity and particle-number superselection analyzed); and, for upper bounds, a particle-number measurement followed by the k-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou, plus a heterodyne stage undoing displacement and squeezing for cold bosonic states.
AI.result: For every fixed β₀>0, the single-copy rate is Θ(m³/ε²) with a lower-bound constant independent of β₀ (no warm regime). At the maximally mixed state, block protocols with at most k copies give N > m³/(8,553,600·k·ε²) for all ε ≤ 1/3600; the exact maximal-block-Fisher formula shows the mt² budget is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size (whether 1/k is the true rate is open). Near the vacuum, block protocols need Ω(m³/(ε²·min{√k,m})) copies with no logarithm. Parity superselection changes no rate; number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs.
AI.conclusion: The bosonic cold/warm crossover has no fermionic analogue. The exterior-power embedding yields matching upper bounds: the particle-number-plus-Nayak–Zhou protocol attains the lower bound for all k on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states (bounded fugacity trace) and on passive bosonic Gaussian states (bounded photon number), and a heterodyne stage extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states, closing the k-entangled gap on the cold class. Intermediate temperatures remain open.

title: Unifying First-Order Coherence, Concurrence, and Bell Correlations in Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
summary: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

AI.tldr: The paper derives exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and maximal CHSH value for coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations, modeled as a three-qubit single-excitation state, and applies them to vacuum propagation for electron and muon preparations.
AI.motivation: Neutrino oscillations offer a natural arena for probing the quantum character of flavor conversion and how quantum resources are distributed over macroscopic distances, motivating exact, tractable quantifiers of coherence and nonlocal correlations in this system.
AI.method: The evolving neutrino is mapped to a three-qubit single-excitation state; the generally mixed two-qubit reduced density matrices are derived, and exact relations are established between squared first-order coherence, squared pairwise concurrence, and the maximal CHSH value, with the CHSH branch structure analyzed via the correlation-tensor spectrum.
AI.result: The squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode plus its two associated squared concurrences sums to unity. The maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair obeys a closed two-branch relation set by its average first-order coherence and concurrence, yielding exact CHSH-violation conditions. For the considered vacuum parameters, electron preparation gives weak violations in electron-containing pairs, whereas muon preparation yields a dominant mu-tau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations; the third-flavor contribution accounts for the differing locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify how quantum correlations are distributed during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extending the framework to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

title: Quantum simulation of classical RCL circuits via complexification and Schrödingerization
summary: The decomplexification procedure establishes a mathematical equivalence between finite dimensional quantum dynamics and classical dynamics by mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one. Its inverse process, complexification --- which lifts a classical dynamics to an equivalent quantum formulation --- is of great interest, particularly because it enables the quantum simulation of equations that are of classical relevance. In this way, one can prepare the solution of classical differential equations to be implemented using quantum computation tools. In the present work, we recall the decomplexification procedure and also discuss several distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations, so as to obtain the corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews the decomplexification procedure linking finite-dimensional quantum and classical dynamics, and discusses several strategies for the inverse complexification of classical equations to obtain equivalent quantum dynamics, enabling quantum simulation of classically relevant differential equations.
AI.motivation: Complexification, the inverse of decomplexification, is attractive because lifting classical dynamics to an equivalent quantum formulation allows the solutions of classical differential equations to be computed via quantum computation tools.
AI.method: The authors recall the decomplexification procedure—mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one to establish equivalence between finite-dimensional quantum and classical dynamics—and then present and discuss several distinct strategies for complexifying classical equations into quantum-equivalent dynamics.
AI.result: Multiple distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations are identified and discussed, yielding corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Complexification provides a route for converting classical differential equations into quantum formulations, thereby enabling their solutions to be prepared and implemented using quantum computation tools.

title: Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable
summary: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.

AI.tldr: Frustration-freeness is decidable for fixed local dimension via a finite system-size cutoff, yet there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness is unprovable in ZFC; the two reconcile because the cutoff is uncomputable as a function of local Hilbert space dimension.
AI.motivation: Frustration-freeness (ground states simultaneously minimize all local terms) underlies paradigmatic models like AKLT and the toric code, and deciding whether a Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes is a fundamental open question. The paper aims to characterize the decidability and provability of this decision problem.
AI.method: The authors analyze the decision problem of frustration-freeness for all system sizes, proving a finite Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension, and constructing a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness is independent of ZFC. They reconcile the results by showing the cutoff is uncomputable as a function of local dimension.
AI.result: Frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension (frustration-freeness at the finite cutoff guarantees it at all sizes); there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved in ZFC; the cutoff is finite per dimension but uncomputable as a function of that dimension.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals a fundamental distinction between decidability and provability in quantum many-body physics: a problem can be decidable yet contain instances whose proof lies beyond standard mathematical axioms, mediated by the uncomputability of the finite cutoff.

title: Fidelity Determines the Minimum Error of Quantum Recovery
summary: Even a recovery that maximizes worst-input entanglement fidelity can retain avoidable errors in subsequent measurements. Entanglement fidelity is the probability of passing a test of whether the state and its entanglement were preserved; infidelity is the probability of failing it. Operational error is the largest possible change in any measurement probability, quantified by the normalized diamond distance. For every finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, we prove that operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity have the same minimum over all recovery operations. The proof constructs one final unitary (a reversible quantum operation) that makes any recovery's operational error no greater than its original worst-input entanglement infidelity. With a retained noise record, we determine the optimal error and characterize all optimal decoders subject to a Kraus-rank limit for each outcome. For a fixed decoded channel, a semidefinite program finds the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. We characterize all optimal final corrections and show that, at a fixed error floor $0<ε<1$, the operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size $s$ is at worst of order $s^{4/3}$, while the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity.

AI.tldr: For any finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, the minimum operational error (normalized diamond distance) over recoveries equals the minimum worst-input entanglement infidelity. A single final unitary can make any recovery's operational error no greater than its worst-input entanglement infidelity, and optimal decoders/corrections are characterized, with optimizers showing $s^{4/3}$ sensitivity to residual unitary errors versus quadratic for the polar correction.
AI.motivation: Recovery operations that maximize worst-input entanglement fidelity can still leave avoidable errors in later measurements, because entanglement fidelity measures only preservation of a test state and its entanglement, not the largest change in measurement statistics. The paper aims to close this gap by relating entanglement infidelity to operational error.
AI.method: Proves equality of the minima of operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity over all recoveries by constructing one final unitary (reversible operation) that bounds any recovery's operational error by its original worst-input entanglement infidelity. With a retained noise record, derives the optimal error and characterizes all optimal decoders under a per-outcome Kraus-rank limit; uses a semidefinite program to find the optimal final unitary for a fixed decoded channel in the low-error regime; characterizes all optimal final corrections and analyzes their sensitivity to residual unitary errors.
AI.result: Operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity share the same minimum over recoveries. Optimal error and all optimal decoders (subject to Kraus-rank limits) are characterized when a noise record is retained; an SDP yields the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. At a fixed error floor $0<\epsilon<1$, operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size $s$ is at worst order $s^{4/3}$, whereas the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-fidelity-optimal recovery is operationally near-optimal under a suitable final unitary, and the resulting optimizers are more robust to residual unitary errors than the polar correction, giving a sharper operational foundation for quantum error correction benchmarks.

title: Operational Characterizations and Resource Structure of the Interactive Weight of Quantum Instruments
summary: Quantifying the interactivity of quantum instruments is fundamental to understanding their resource structure and operational capabilities. Here, we introduce the interactive weight of quantum instruments as a resource quantifier that measures the minimum fraction of an instrument that cannot be explained by non-interactive components. Through quantum-information tasks including quantum-state recovery, positive linear loss games, and environment-assisted input-blind extraction, we establish quantitative bounds on the interactive weight of quantum instruments and exact operational characterizations of its complementary quantity, the maximal non-interactive content. In particular, we extend environment-assisted input-blind extraction to the setting of restricted environmental access and develop a corresponding framework. Within the allowed-operations framework introduced by Hsieh et al., we establish fundamental resource-theoretic properties of the interactive weight of quantum instruments, including faithfulness, convexity, and monotonicity under deterministic allowed operations. Furthermore, we prove that the maximal non-interactive content satisfies exact multiplicativity under independent parallel composition, yielding necessary constraints on multicopy resource conversion and establishing the finite-copy maximal-weight distillation no-go result under deterministic allowed operations. These results establish a unified theoretical framework for the interactive weight of quantum instruments from the perspectives of resource quantification, operational interpretation, and resource conversion, providing systematic theoretical tools for the quantitative comparison and conversion of interactive quantum instruments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "interactive weight" of quantum instruments — the minimum fraction of an instrument that cannot be explained by non-interactive components — and provides operational characterizations, resource-theoretic properties, and conversion constraints for it.
AI.motivation: Quantifying the interactivity of quantum instruments is fundamental for understanding their resource structure and operational capabilities, but a dedicated resource quantifier for instrument interactivity was lacking.
AI.method: Defines interactive weight as a resource quantifier for quantum instruments; uses quantum-information tasks (quantum-state recovery, positive linear loss games, environment-assisted input-blind extraction, including a restricted-environmental-access extension) to derive bounds and exact characterizations of the complementary maximal non-interactive content; analyzes properties within the allowed-operations framework of Hsieh et al.
AI.result: Establishes quantitative bounds on interactive weight and exact operational characterizations of maximal non-interactive content; proves faithfulness, convexity, and monotonicity under deterministic allowed operations; proves exact multiplicativity of maximal non-interactive content under independent parallel composition, yielding necessary constraints on multicopy resource conversion and a finite-copy maximal-weight distillation no-go result.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified framework for interactive weight of quantum instruments spanning resource quantification, operational interpretation, and resource conversion, offering systematic tools for quantitative comparison and conversion of interactive quantum instruments.

title: Spin-Exchange-Controlled Nonclassical Light in Cavity Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
summary: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.

AI.tldr: Two three-level emitters in a ring cavity, coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, allow selective suppression of two-photon excitation via EIT dark-state polaritons, yielding tunable photon blockade and switchable antibunching/bunching controlled by exchange strength and cavity-coupling phase.
AI.motivation: Controlling nonclassical light while keeping a finite cavity response requires selectively suppressing unwanted multiphoton excitation—i.e., achieving photon blockade that is tunable and does not rely on strong single-emitter nonlinearity alone.
AI.method: A ring-cavity system with two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance and modifies the dressed two-photon excitation pathways; the exchange strength, control-field strength, and relative cavity-coupling phase are tuned to control the one- and two-photon transition amplitudes.
AI.result: Strong photon antibunching appears when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. Joint tuning of exchange interaction and control-field strength sustains pronounced photon blockade with finite intracavity population over an extended interaction range. The relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, switching photon statistics between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength.
