AI.conclusion: Coherent control of collective excitation pathways in an exchange-coupled EIT ring-cavity system offers a viable route to tunable nonclassical-light sources, with photon statistics switchable via the cavity-coupling phase.

title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
summary: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $Ω_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $Ω_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.

AI.tldr: Rydberg-exposed entangling gates in neutral atoms cannot reduce the product Ω_max·T_R below 2.9312 in the perfect-blockade regime, regardless of pulse shape or duration; a matching pulse with Ω_max·T_R<2.9359 is certified, leaving a gap under 0.16%.
AI.motivation: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates but causes spontaneous decay. It was unresolved whether pulse shaping and longer gate times can make this Rydberg exposure arbitrarily small; the paper asks whether an irreducible minimum exposure exists.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound on Ω_max·T_R (max Rabi frequency times average Rydberg dwell time) for an exact single-global-laser controlled-Z gate in the perfect-blockade regime, using a sum-of-squares certificate tightened by shared-drive constraints, plus interval arithmetic to certify an explicit near-optimal gate pulse.
AI.result: Ω_max·T_R is bounded below by 2.9312 independent of pulse shape and duration; a pulse achieving Ω_max·T_R<2.9359 is certified, so the bounds differ by less than 0.16%.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental, irreducible cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics; the bound is an exact-gate benchmark for evaluating future gate-control strategies.

title: Higher-order topological quantum battery
summary: A quantum battery is a next-generation energy-storage device that exploits genuinely quantum properties such as superposition and coherence. We propose a second-order topological quantum battery coupled to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model, where optical loss is present on all lattice sites while nonlinear gains are introduced selectively at the output sites. Under these realistic non-Hermitian conditions, the system exhibits a clear topological phase transition manifested in both the ergotropy and the charging power. Remarkably, perfect work extraction is realized in the topological phase, where the maximum value of the ergotropy is quantized and acts as a good topological-phase indicator. The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, where mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization gives rise to collective energy storage.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a second-order topological quantum battery coupled to a nonlinear, non-Hermitian breathing-Kagome photonic crystal and show that ergotropy and charging power signal a topological phase transition, with quantized perfect work extraction in the topological phase.
AI.motivation: Quantum batteries that exploit genuine quantum features (superposition, coherence) are attractive as next-generation energy storage, but realizing them under realistic loss and gain conditions while exploiting topological robustness remains an open challenge.
AI.method: A second-order topological quantum battery is coupled to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model. Realistic non-Hermitian conditions are imposed: optical loss on all sites plus selective nonlinear gain at the output sites. Ergotropy and charging power are computed across the topological phase transition, and the triangular geometry is used to distribute energy into two batteries via mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization.
AI.result: A clear topological phase transition appears in both the ergotropy and the charging power. In the topological phase, perfect work extraction is achieved and the maximum ergotropy is quantized, serving as a reliable topological-phase indicator. The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, yielding collective energy storage through mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization.
AI.conclusion: Second-order topology combined with non-Hermitian gain/loss engineering provides a robust route to high-performance quantum batteries, with quantized ergotropy as a topological diagnostic and symmetry-protected synchronization enabling collective energy storage.

title: Weak Values in Postselected Quantum Trajectories
summary: Weak value (WV) describes the amplified response of a meter when the measured system undergoes postselection. While conventional WV theory mainly rests on a single system-meter interaction setting, it remains unexplored whether WV can act as an effective pointer for sequential quantum measurements under postselection. Here we introduce the concept of WVs to the setting of sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories. We find that WV naturally emerges in postselected quantum trajectories of sequential weak measurements, by establishing a connection between the WV of the measured observable and the postselected statistics of quantum trajectories. Using sequential weak measurements on a qubit or an oscillator implemented by Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit, we show that postselection shifts the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned ones, with an effective bias described by the WV. Our predictions are feasible to test in various platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper extends weak value (WV) theory from a single system-meter interaction to sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories, showing that WV naturally emerges as an effective bias of postselected trajectory statistics.
AI.motivation: Conventional WV theory rests mainly on a single system-meter interaction setting; whether WV can act as an effective pointer for sequential quantum measurements under postselection remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce WV concepts into sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories, linking the WV of the measured observable to postselected statistics of quantum trajectories. They analyze sequential weak measurements on a qubit or oscillator implemented via Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit.
AI.result: Postselection shifts the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned one, with an effective bias described by the WV. Predictions are feasible to test across various platforms.
AI.conclusion: WV serves as an effective pointer for postselected sequential quantum measurements, connecting weak-value theory to quantum trajectory statistics and offering experimentally testable signatures.

title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
summary:
Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$.
  Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources.
  Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a quantum analogue of the Bennett-Gill question: if UP ⊄ BQP, then NP^O ∩ coNP^O ⊄ BQP^O with probability 1 over a random oracle O. It also shows a black-box barrier ruling out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case hardness in NP ∩ coNP to post-quantum injective OWFs and iO, indicating the non-black-box techniques are essential.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions—specifically, whether NP ∩ coNP (hard languages with two-sided certification) remains hard relative to a random oracle (the Bennett-Gill question). This matters quantumly because Shor's algorithms break number-theoretic hardness, while leading post-quantum assumptions (lattices, etc.) do not directly yield hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. A quantum analogue would provide evidence that structured quantum hardness can emerge from unstructured sources despite these gaps.
AI.method: Conditional oracle separation via random-oracle techniques: assume UP ⊄ BQP and prove NP^O ∩ coNP^O ⊄ BQP^O with probability 1 over random O. Complementarily, prove an impossibility result—a fully black-box barrier against quantum reductions from worst-case quantum hardness in NP ∩ coNP to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. The first result relies on non-black-box techniques, which the barrier result shows to be necessary.
AI.result: Under UP ⊄ BQP, NP^O ∩ coNP^O ⊄ BQP^O holds with probability 1 over a random oracle O, extending the classical conditional affirmative answer of [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] to the quantum setting. Additionally, no fully black-box quantum reduction exists from worst-case quantum hardness in NP ∩ coNP to post-quantum injective OWFs or iO.
AI.conclusion: Structured quantum hardness (two-sided-certifiable hard languages) can plausibly arise from unstructured assumptions, conditional on UP ⊄ BQP. The black-box barrier excludes a broad class of generic approaches to deriving such hardness from standard cryptographic primitives, giving partial evidence that non-black-box techniques are essential to the separation.

title: Information flow control in hybrid quantum networks
summary: Quantum resources can change the dynamical features and operational behaviors of conventional networks. Long-distance entanglement supports information transfer between nodes lacking a direct connection. This entanglement link not only modifies the stationary effective connectivity of the network but can also be used to suppress undesirable classical dynamics. By examining information flow control mechanism, we demonstrate that classical collective behavior can be well-balanced by altering the initially distributed entanglement. We show the entanglement thresholds for two distinct control approaches: linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability.

AI.tldr: Distributed long-distance entanglement acts as a controllable resource to regulate and balance classical collective dynamics in networks, with thresholds derived for two control strategies.
AI.motivation: Quantum resources, especially long-distance entanglement, can alter the dynamical and operational behavior of conventional (classical) networks. The authors aim to show that entanglement links can be exploited not only to reshape stationary effective connectivity but also to suppress unwanted classical dynamics, motivating a systematic study of how initially distributed entanglement can be tuned to balance collective behavior.
AI.method: The authors analyze an information-flow control mechanism in networks where long-distance entanglement provides links between nodes without direct connections, modifying effective connectivity. They evaluate two distinct control approaches—linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability—and derive entanglement thresholds required for each to achieve control.
AI.result: Classical collective behavior can be well-balanced by altering the initially distributed entanglement. Entanglement thresholds are identified for both linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability.
AI.conclusion: Distributed entanglement is an effective control knob for classical network dynamics, and the derived thresholds specify how much entanglement is needed under each control scheme to balance collective behavior.

title: Elimination of quantum causal confusion in the presence of dual states
summary: There is a rich class of bipartite quantum correlations between qubits which are consistent both with measurements performed in parallel and measurements performed in sequence. This phenomenon has recently been termed \emph{quantum causal confusion}, which is made mathematically precise by the notion of a dual state---a bipartite density operator whose associated correlations are causally ambiguous. A natural question is then whether or not the spatial and temporal scenarios associated with a dual state are fundamentally indistinguishable from a causal perspective. Here we show that as long as the reduced density operator of a dual state is oblique---meaning that all coefficients in its Pauli expansion are non-zero---then the underlying joint probabilities giving rise to such causally ambiguous correlations will differ in the spatial and temporal scenarios. Specifically, the temporal joint probabilities will inherently violate the no-signalling condition, thus eliminating quantum causal confusion. Moreover, as oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, the elimination of quantum causal confusion is the norm rather than an exception.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that quantum causal confusion—bipartite qubit correlations consistent with both parallel and sequential measurements—is eliminated whenever the dual state's reduced density operator is "oblique" (all Pauli coefficients non-zero), because the temporal joint probabilities then violate no-signalling. Since oblique states are open and dense in the Bloch ball, such confusion is the exception rather than the norm.
AI.motivation: A recently identified class of bipartite qubit correlations can be reproduced in both spatial (parallel) and temporal (sequential) measurement scenarios, formalized via "dual states" whose correlations are causally ambiguous. The open question is whether the spatial and temporal descriptions of a dual state are fundamentally indistinguishable from a causal standpoint, i.e., whether the underlying joint probabilities genuinely differ between the two scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce the notion of an oblique reduced density operator, defined as one whose Pauli expansion has all non-zero coefficients, and analyze the joint probability distributions generated by a dual state in both the spatial and temporal measurement scenarios. They examine the no-signalling condition for the temporal joint probabilities under this obliqueness condition and assess the measure-theoretic size of oblique states within the Bloch ball.
AI.result: For any dual state whose reduced density operator is oblique, the underlying joint probabilities differ between the spatial and temporal scenarios: the temporal joint probabilities inherently violate the no-signalling condition. This eliminates the causal ambiguity. Because oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, this elimination holds generically.
AI.conclusion: Quantum causal confusion is the exception rather than the norm: for generic (oblique) dual states the spatial and temporal scenarios are causally distinguishable through violation of no-signalling in the temporal joint probabilities. The result reframes causally ambiguous correlations as a measure-zero, non-generic phenomenon.

title: Bell Test and Quantum State-Space Geometry
summary: We explore a minimal phenomenological model of coupling between the geometry of the classical spacetime and the quantum state space. Assuming a simple structure of the combined manifold, bilinear interaction between the corresponding geometric scalars and the simplest case of the two-qubit entanglement dynamics, we derive an illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant from the requirement of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality violation over a finite time interval.

AI.tldr: The authors construct a minimal phenomenological model in which classical spacetime geometry couples bilinearly to quantum state-space geometry, and use two-qubit entanglement dynamics plus CHSH violation over a finite time window to bound the geometric coupling constant.
AI.motivation: There is no established quantitative link between the geometry of classical spacetime and the geometry of quantum state space; the paper seeks a minimal, tractable framework to parametrize such a coupling and to derive an empirically meaningful constraint on its strength.
AI.method: A minimal phenomenological model based on a simple product/composite structure of the combined manifold. Geometric scalars of the classical spacetime and of the quantum state space are coupled through a bilinear interaction term, and the dynamics of two-qubit entanglement is treated as the simplest illustrative case. The geometric coupling constant is then constrained by requiring that the CHSH inequality remain violated over a finite time interval.
AI.result: An illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant is obtained from the requirement of sustained CHSH violation across a finite time interval.
AI.conclusion: CHSH-type nonlocality over finite times provides a viable phenomenological probe for bounding spacetime–state-space geometric coupling; the framework is minimal and illustrative rather than a full theory.

title: Efficient Pauli Truncation from Operator Stabilizer Rényi Entropy
summary: Operator stabilizer Rényi entropy (OSE) quantifies the magic of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of their compressibility in the Pauli basis. We establish rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be efficiently approximated by Pauli truncation in terms of the scaling of its OSE. Specifically, we prove that volume-law scaling of OSE for $α\geq1$ prevents efficient Pauli truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error. On the other hand, logarithmic growth of OSE for $0<α<1/2$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation approximability uniformly over all states. A counterexample shows that this sufficient range cannot be extended on the basis of OSE scaling alone. If we restrict to correlations over suitable low-average state ensembles, then the sufficient range extends to $0<α<1$. We further derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and approximation guarantees for fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators. Moreover, under an independent-sign assumption, we show that logarithmic OSE for $0<α<1$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation with the prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding when operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation and for guiding the development of classical simulation methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proves rigorous bounds connecting the scaling of operator stabilizer Rényi entropy (OSE) of Heisenberg operators to whether those operators admit efficient Pauli truncation (compressibility in the Pauli basis).
AI.motivation: OSE quantifies operator magic and is proposed as a diagnostic of Pauli-basis compressibility, but no rigorous link existed between OSE scaling and the feasibility of efficiently approximating operators via Pauli truncation. The work aims to establish when operator magic constrains or enables efficient classical simulation.
AI.method: The authors derive rigorous bounds relating OSE scaling to approximation error of Pauli truncation: they prove a negative result that volume-law OSE for α≥1 prevents efficient truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error, and positive results that logarithmic OSE guarantees efficient truncation (for 0<α<1/2 uniformly over all states; extending to 0<α<1 over low-average state ensembles). They provide a counterexample limiting the sufficient range based on OSE alone, derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation, give approximation guarantees for fixed-order OTOCs, and analyze an independent-sign assumption yielding high-probability guarantees for logarithmic OSE with 0<α<1.
AI.result: Volume-law OSE (α≥1) obstructs efficient Pauli truncation; logarithmic OSE for 0<α<1/2 guarantees uniform efficient approximability across all states; the sufficient range cannot be extended from OSE scaling alone (counterexample); over suitable low-average ensembles the range extends to 0<α<1; cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and fixed-order OTOC guarantees are obtained; under an independent-sign assumption, logarithmic OSE with 0<α<1 gives efficient truncation at prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability.
AI.conclusion: The results supply a theoretical framework clarifying when operator magic (OSE scaling) constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation, and offer guidance for developing and assessing classical simulation methods based on Pauli propagation.

title: Optimal quantum metrology with restricted controls
summary: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-$1/2$ examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.

AI.tldr: Optimal control theory (Pontryagin maximum principle) is used to maximize quantum Fisher information under bounded-amplitude multi-channel Hamiltonian controls, revealing how time-dependent waveforms beat optimized constant control and CPMG pulses in two spin-1/2 sensing scenarios.
AI.motivation: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but attainable precision is limited by fixed probe preparation and restricted control resources; there is a need to determine what precision is experimentally reachable under such constraints.
AI.method: Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, the authors formulate maximization of quantum Fisher information at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels under a weighted amplitude constraint; the formulation extends to stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations, and a geometric description of sensitivity accumulation is derived to explain the optimized protocols.
AI.result: Two spin-1/2 examples show enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, and optimized waveforms improve on CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources is essential for improving experimentally attainable precision; the PMP-based framework provides both optimal waveforms and geometric insight into sensitivity accumulation.

title: Observing mixed-state Uhlmann winding numbers in integrated photonic quantum walks
summary: Integer winding numbers provide a well-established classification of topological phases protected by chiral symmetry at zero temperature, but extending this classification to thermal mixed states remains challenging. The Uhlmann phase, a mixed-state extension of the Berry phase, provides a geometric framework for characterizing finite-temperature topology. However, this geometric phase is restricted to two quantized values and therefore cannot resolve the multiple thermal regimes associated with high winding numbers. Here, we experimentally observe integer mixed-state winding numbers in a photonic quantum-walk chip. We prepare and reconstruct thermal states associated with high-winding chiral Hamiltonians and their spectrum-preserving dimensional extensions. The reconstructed Uhlmann overlaps form closed trajectories in the complex plane, and their integer windings around the zero-overlap point are directly observed. As temperature increases, the Uhlmann winding number undergoes multiple discrete changes, accompanied by switches of the Uhlmann phase and the successive disappearance of momentum-resolved topological kinks. These results highlight an integer-valued topological characterization alongside the mixed-state geometric phase.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally observe integer mixed-state winding numbers via the Uhlmann phase in a photonic quantum-walk chip, resolving thermal regimes of high-winding chiral Hamiltonians beyond the two-valued Uhlmann phase.
AI.motivation: Integer winding numbers classify chiral-symmetric topological phases at zero temperature, but extending this to thermal mixed states is difficult. The Uhlmann phase, a mixed-state analog of the Berry phase, gives a geometric framework but is restricted to two quantized values, so it cannot resolve the multiple thermal regimes of high winding numbers.
AI.method: Thermal states associated with high-winding chiral Hamiltonians and their spectrum-preserving dimensional extensions are prepared and reconstructed on a photonic quantum-walk chip. Uhlmann overlaps are measured, forming closed trajectories in the complex plane whose integer winding around the zero-overlap point is directly observed.
AI.result: Integer mixed-state winding numbers are directly observed. As temperature rises, the Uhlmann winding number undergoes multiple discrete changes, accompanied by switches of the Uhlmann phase and successive disappearance of momentum-resolved topological kinks.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an integer-valued topological characterization that complements the mixed-state geometric phase, extending winding-number classification to finite-temperature mixed states.

title: Separability and lower bounds of concurrence via symmetric measurement correlations
summary: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement is a central issue in quantum information science, particularly for unknown quantum states. Based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices, we present a family of separability criteria that can be experimentally applied without state tomography, and recover some related existing criteria as special cases. Using the constructed correlation matrices, we further derive a class of lower bounds of concurrence. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that our criteria outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and that the obtained lower bounds on concurrence are tighter than known counterparts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a family of separability criteria derived from symmetric measurement correlation matrices that require no state tomography, generalizing existing criteria, and further derives a class of concurrence lower bounds that outperform/tighten known counterparts.
AI.motivation: Detecting and quantifying entanglement is central to quantum information, especially for unknown states, but most criteria demand full state tomography which is experimentally costly. There is a need for experimentally practical, tomographic-free criteria with improved detection power.
AI.method: Constructs symmetric measurement correlation matrices and, from them, a family of separability criteria applicable without state tomography; recovers related existing criteria as special cases. The same correlation matrices are used to derive a class of lower bounds on concurrence.
AI.result: Via illustrative examples, the criteria are shown to outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and the derived concurrence lower bounds are shown to be tighter than known counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Symmetric measurement correlation matrices provide a unifying, experimentally accessible framework for both entanglement detection and concurrence quantification, with demonstrable advantages over existing approaches.

title: Efficient preparation of spin-squeezed states with Grover's algorithm
summary: We propose a scheme for preparing spin-squeezed states in an ensemble of $N$ spin-$1/2$ particles based on Grover's algorithm. With only a few oracles, the scheme can exactly prepare superpositions of a few neighboring Dicke states with the Wineland squeezing parameter scaling as $N^{-1}$. The scheme requires only global rotations and Dicke-selective phase shifts, thus avoiding the need to engineer a dedicated many-body Hamiltonian for the squeezing dynamics. We further discuss the feasibility of realizing the scheme in cavity QED systems, with the phase-matched Grover iterations realized by single-photon reflection from a dispersively coupled cavity. Full-sequence scattering calculations accounting for finite photon bandwidth and loss show that appreciable spin squeezing can be achieved with high fidelity for suitable system parameters.

AI.tldr: A Grover-algorithm-based scheme prepares spin-squeezed states in an ensemble of N spin-1/2 particles using only a few oracles and global operations, achieving Wineland squeezing parameter scaling as N^{-1}.
AI.motivation: Spin squeezing is typically produced by engineering dedicated many-body Hamiltonians, which is demanding. The authors seek a simpler control scheme that avoids such Hamiltonian engineering while achieving strong squeezing.
AI.method: Grover iterations are used to prepare exact superpositions of a few neighboring Dicke states, requiring only global rotations and Dicke-selective phase shifts (no tailored many-body Hamiltonian). Feasibility is analyzed in cavity QED, where phase-matched Grover iterations are realized via single-photon reflection from a dispersively coupled cavity, with full-sequence scattering calculations including finite photon bandwidth and loss.
AI.result: With only a few oracles, the scheme exactly prepares superpositions of neighboring Dicke states with Wineland squeezing parameter scaling as N^{-1}. Scattering calculations with finite bandwidth and loss show appreciable spin squeezing achievable with high fidelity for suitable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Grover-based control offers a Hamiltonian-free route to strong (Heisenberg-scaling) spin squeezing and is feasible in cavity QED with realistic parameters, providing a practical alternative to engineered squeezing dynamics.

title: Observation of Inter-Transition Interference
summary: Many well-known quantum interference phenomena are associated with coherent superpositions of quantum states. Recent theoretical work showed that dissipative coupling between transition coherences can give rise to a distinct form of quantum interference in open quantum systems, termed inter-transition interference (ITI). Here we experimentally observe ITI through coherent microwave reflection spectroscopy of a superconducting artificial atom realized by a Kerr parametric oscillator. Using strong parametric driving, we access a regime in which two transitions become nearly degenerate and simultaneously contribute to the reflected response. The observed spectral lineshapes are not adequately captured by a model of independent transitions. By contrast, theoretical calculations that incorporate dissipative coupling between the corresponding transition coherences reproduce the essential features of the measured spectra. These results provide experimental evidence for ITI and demonstrate that dissipative coupling between transition coherences can qualitatively modify spectroscopic responses. More broadly, our work identifies transition coherences as a new arena for quantum interference in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: First experimental observation of inter-transition interference (ITI) via microwave reflection spectroscopy of a Kerr parametric oscillator, showing dissipative coupling between transition coherences qualitatively reshapes spectra beyond independent-transition models.
AI.motivation: Recent theory predicts that dissipative coupling between transition coherences in open quantum systems produces a distinct interference phenomenon (inter-transition interference, ITI) not captured by independent-transition descriptions; this work aims to provide the missing experimental evidence.
AI.method: Coherent microwave reflection spectroscopy on a superconducting artificial atom implemented as a Kerr parametric oscillator. Strong parametric driving brings two transitions into near-degeneracy so both contribute simultaneously to the reflected response. Measured lineshapes are compared with an independent-transition model and with calculations incorporating dissipative coupling between the transition coherences.
AI.result: The independent-transition model fails to reproduce the measured spectral lineshapes, whereas the theory including dissipative coherence coupling captures the essential spectral features, providing experimental evidence for ITI.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative coupling between transition coherences can qualitatively modify spectroscopic responses, establishing transition coherences as a new arena for quantum interference in open quantum systems.

title: Detecting Nonbilocal Correlations via Parameterized Elegant Joint Measurement
summary: Quantum networks constitute a defining resource for quantum information processing; however, their nonclassical behavior is jointly governed by the choice of measurement basis and the independence of the distributed sources. We study a bilocal entanglement-swapping network in which the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM). For two independent Bell-state sources, we construct two binary edge observables and then derive a quantum prediction involving three parameters, which surpasses the classical constraints. In particular, the parameter θ controls both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction. These results provide an analytic and directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.

AI.tldr: A bilocal entanglement-swapping network with a three-parameter elegant joint measurement is analyzed; two binary edge observables yield a quantum prediction exceeding classical (bilocal) bounds, tunable via the EJM entanglement parameter θ.
AI.motivation: Nonclassical behavior in quantum networks depends jointly on measurement-basis choice and source independence, so understanding how basis parameters control nonbilocality in a two-source network is needed.
AI.method: Constructs a bilocal entanglement-swapping network where the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM) on two independent Bell-state sources; defines two binary edge observables and derives an analytic quantum prediction with three parameters to compare against classical/bilocal constraints.
AI.result: The derived quantum prediction surpasses the classical constraints; the parameter θ governs both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction.
AI.conclusion: Provides an analytic, directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.

title: Development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy using heralded emission spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials
summary: Organic light-emitting materials are widely used in optoelectronics and bioimaging, but sometimes conventional fluorescence spectroscopy techniques can be limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up and photobleaching. We report a quantum-spectroscopic approach using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection, to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities. We demonstrate this approach across three organic light-emitting material classes: the fluorescent dye Rhodamine 6G, an organic semiconducting conjugated polymer poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), and a fluorescent protein mOrange. The intrinsic timing correlation between signal and idler photons enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Across all materials and integration times of 500, 1000 and 3600 seconds, heralded detection yields signal-to-noise ratios 1.6-3.0 times higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range. For MEH-PPV, this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Our measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical pulsed-laser reference values.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates quantum-spectroscopic photoluminescence lifetime measurements on three organic light-emitting materials using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs with heralded detection, achieving 1.6-3.0× higher SNR than attenuated classical pulsed-laser excitation.
AI.motivation: Conventional fluorescence spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials is limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up, and photobleaching; a low-excitation-intensity, background-suppressing alternative is needed.
AI.method: Frequency-entangled nondegenerate photon pairs generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection are used to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities; intrinsic signal-idler timing correlation enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Validated on Rhodamine 6G, MEH-PPV, and mOrange at integration times of 500, 1000, and 3600 s.
AI.result: Heralded detection yields SNRs 1.6-3.0× higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range; for MEH-PPV this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical reference values.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-correlated heralded photon-pair spectroscopy provides a low-intensity, background-robust route to accurate photoluminescence lifetime determination across fluorescent dyes, conjugated polymers, and fluorescent proteins.

title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
summary: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.

AI.tldr: Fermionic composite bosons can appear elementary or composite depending on the probe; Weyl-defect and binned observables diagnose this differently, and a spectral filter plus polar correction lets one herald a logical singlet from two copies of the composite.
AI.motivation: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another, so a single criterion of compositeness is insufficient; the paper seeks to compare different probes of the same paired-mode model and to establish which observables reliably expose the underlying fermionic algebra.
AI.method: Exactly solvable paired-mode model compared across three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations g^(2). The Weyl defect is derived with an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in Schmidt moments; binned observables are analyzed as piecewise-constant functions of Schmidt weights with sensitivity to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges. A spectral filter and polar correction construct an exact Pauli algebra, and a heralded joint projection extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies.
AI.result: The Weyl defect behaves well: exact product form and dilute Schmidt-moment expansion. Binned observables are piecewise constant, sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges, and on the flat-spectrum ladder converge slowly and nonmonotonically. The filtered construction yields an exact Pauli algebra, and the heralded joint projection succeeds at the percent level in finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three despite order-one Weyl defects. Near-unit g^(2) does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart with strictly positive vacuum overlap at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes convergence holds at all but countably many filter cutoffs, with positivity at the studied cutoffs left open.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing compositeness is probe-dependent: the Weyl defect admits a clean analytic treatment while binned statistics are brittle and g^(2) near unity is not a sufficient witness. A spectral filter with polar correction recovers an exact Pauli algebra and enables heralded singlet extraction from two copies, with convergence guaranteed for flat spectra and almost everywhere for infinite summable-amplitude spectra, while positivity at the filter cutoffs remains an open question.

title: Constrained Quantum Imaginary Time in Krylov Space
summary:
We introduce constrained quantum imaginary time evolution (CQITE), extending quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to constrained-search dynamics for ground-state preparation with prescribed expectation-value constraints. A central challenge in practical QITE is constructing a compact unitary representation of the imaginary-time evolution while maintaining accuracy and controlling the approximation error.
  We resolve this challenge by deriving an exact characterization of the imaginary-time evolution from the Krylov space generated by repeated applications of the Hamiltonian to the initial state. This characterization induces a hierarchy of operator directions expressed through nested anti-commutators. Truncating the hierarchy produces a systematic static operator pool, with polynomial size in the system size at any fixed truncation order. The resulting construction provides a principled route to compact unitary approximations of imaginary-time dynamics.
  Numerical tests on spin models show close agreement with exact constrained imaginary-time evolution and small constraint deviations, while a fermionic example yields energies close to the analytic constrained-search reference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces constrained quantum imaginary time evolution (CQITE) and resolves the compact-unitary construction challenge by deriving an exact Krylov-space characterization of imaginary-time evolution, yielding a truncatable, polynomially sized static operator pool.
AI.motivation: Practical QITE struggles to build a compact unitary representation of imaginary-time evolution while preserving accuracy and controlling approximation error; the authors also want to extend QITE to constrained-search dynamics for ground-state preparation under prescribed expectation-value constraints.
AI.method: CQITE extends QITE to constrained-search dynamics. The authors derive an exact characterization of imaginary-time evolution from the Krylov space generated by repeated Hamiltonian applications to the initial state, inducing a hierarchy of operator directions via nested anti-commutators. Truncating this hierarchy gives a systematic static operator pool of polynomial size in system size at any fixed truncation order.
AI.result: Numerical tests on spin models show close agreement with exact constrained imaginary-time evolution and small constraint deviations; a fermionic example yields energies close to the analytic constrained-search reference.
AI.conclusion: The Krylov-based truncated hierarchy provides a principled route to compact unitary approximations of imaginary-time dynamics, enabling accurate constrained ground-state preparation with controlled error and scalable operator pools.

title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
summary: We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RDK pulses: a multi-robust quantum control strategy that suppresses multilevel leakage and restores two-level robustness by reformulating the DRAG technique through an iterative quantum KAM algorithm, applied to robust inverse-optimization (RIO) control.
AI.motivation: Qubits embedded in multilevel structures (e.g., superconducting transmons) suffer from leakage out of the computational subspace and from unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. The authors aim to suppress both simultaneously, while still exploiting well-established two-level control designs.
AI.method: A reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique is developed that fully incorporates control pulses originally designed for two-level models, using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. This is combined with robust inverse optimization (RIO) to produce so-called RDK pulses, whose performance is analyzed across pulse durations, iteration counts, and robustness types.
AI.result: Two-level robustness is restored after only a few KAM iterations, following an asymptotic exponential (superasymptotic-series) approximation, even for relatively short pulse durations. The resulting RDK pulses are near-optimal in energy compared with the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace.
AI.conclusion: By effectively reproducing two-level dynamics within a multilevel system, RDK pulses are versatile and compatible with existing two-level control strategies under analyzed conditions of smoothness and duration, making them well suited for superconducting transmons and other qubits embedded in multilevel structures.

title: Continuous variable payload transmitter for the SPOQC mission
summary: The continuous variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme enables two parties to share a secret key separated by a certain distance. Here we propose, design, build, test and show results of a CV payload transmitter, intended to demonstrate downlink based QKD from a CubeSat in low earth orbit. This is part of the SPOQC mission by Quantum Communications Hub, UK which was successfully launched on March 2026.

AI.tldr: Design, build, and test of a continuous-variable QKD payload transmitter for CubeSat downlink quantum key distribution, part of the UK SPOQC mission.
AI.motivation: Continuous-variable QKD enables two parties separated by a distance to share a secret key; demonstrating this from a CubeSat in low earth orbit would validate downlink-based satellite CV-QKD as a practical route to global key distribution.
AI.method: Propose, design, build, and test a CV payload transmitter (optical/source, modulation, and detection-related hardware) intended for downlink QKD from a CubeSat in LEO, integrated as part of the SPOQC mission by the UK Quantum Communications Hub.
AI.result: The payload transmitter was built and experimentally tested, with results reported; the SPOQC mission was successfully launched in March 2026.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a flight-oriented CV-QKD transmitter payload for CubeSat downlink QKD, establishing the hardware basis for space-based continuous-variable quantum key distribution.

title: Negative non-linear differential dissipation in mechanical quartz resonators
summary: We observe negative non-linear differential dissipation in a low-frequency (32.7 kHz) miniature quartz tuning fork, representing a high-Q piezoelectric resonator, at temperatures below 0.3 K. Similar drive-induced dissipation suppression has previously been reported in superconducting microwave resonators, and high-frequency MEMS devices, associated to coupling with tunneling two-level systems (TTLSs). In the case of low-frequency resonators, the equivalent temperature of the mechanical mode is orders of magnitude lower than the thermodynamic temperature of the device, implying that accessible TTLS states are largely saturated. We demonstrate that the observed temperature and drive dependence of the losses fit well within the framework of an interacting TTLS bath, indicating the presence of a channel for energy transfer between the mechanical mode and thermally activated TTLSs. As a possible coupling mechanism, we suggest microwave phonon modes in the metallic electrodes of the tuning fork.

AI.tldr: Observation of negative non-linear differential dissipation in a low-frequency (32.7 kHz) quartz tuning fork below 0.3 K, explained within an interacting tunneling two-level system (TTLS) bath framework.
AI.motivation: Drive-induced dissipation suppression was previously reported in superconducting microwave resonators and high-frequency MEMS, attributed to coupling with TTLSs; the authors test whether analogous behavior exists in a low-frequency high-Q piezoelectric resonator.
AI.method: Low-temperature (below 0.3 K) measurements of a 32.7 kHz miniature quartz tuning fork, analyzing temperature and drive dependence of the losses and comparing to an interacting TTLS bath model; proposing microwave phonon modes in metallic electrodes as a coupling channel.
AI.result: Negative non-linear differential dissipation is observed; the temperature and drive dependence of losses fit well within an interacting TTLS bath framework, indicating an energy-transfer channel between the mechanical mode and thermally activated TTLSs, despite the mechanical mode's equivalent temperature being orders of magnitude below the device temperature.
AI.conclusion: Low-frequency resonators also exhibit TTLS-related dissipation suppression, consistent with an interacting TTLS bath; microwave phonon modes in the metallic electrodes are suggested as the coupling mechanism.

title: Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
comment: 7 pages + 2 pages of appendices, 8 figures, 2 tables
summary: Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: The authors implement a quantum spin-chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on a trapped-ion quantum computer, demonstrating conversion of local particles into non-local string excitations via a duality defect.
AI.motivation: The magnetic monopole paradox, recently resolved using generalized symmetries, motivates exploring non-local excitations such as duality defects and string operators. Quantum hardware now enables observing many-body phenomena, making it timely to realize these generalized-symmetry concepts experimentally.
AI.method: A novel protocol prepares a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. Combining this with time evolution across a duality defect converts local particles into non-local string-like excitations. The approach is implemented on the Quantinuum System Model H2 (trapped-ion) for the transverse-field Ising model and the SPT phase of the cluster model.
AI.result: Particle-to-string conversion is demonstrated in both the transverse-field Ising model and the SPT phase of the cluster model on real quantum hardware, efficiently generating non-local string excitations from local particles.
AI.conclusion: Duality defects and generalized symmetries are established as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware, providing a spin-chain platform for magnetic monopole scattering analogues.

title: Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
comment: This manuscript is the preprint version of an article published in Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy. The final published version is available at: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11433-026-3065-5
summary: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: A novel energy-level engineering technique exploiting the Autler-Townes effect achieves a fast (97 ns), high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) all-microwave CZ gate without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, but current methods are limited: frequency-tuning techniques cause decoherence, while all-microwave schemes face a trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate.
AI.method: The authors introduce an energy-level engineering technique that uses the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate qubit nonlinearity while leaving the computational subspace unperturbed and preserving coherence time.
AI.result: Experimentally validated a fast (97 ns) CZ gate with fidelity 99.40(9)%; error analysis shows gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence.
AI.conclusion: The scheme enables fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and is applicable to various quantum platforms.

title: Crosstalk-Induced Row Hammer Attacks on Quantum Random Access Codes
summary: Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of $60\%$. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the practical relevance of these attacks, we study their impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs), observing a degradation in their average success probabilities.

AI.tldr: Crosstalk-induced attacks are feasible on all tested IBM and IQM superconducting quantum processors, with victim-qubit outcome-flip probabilities up to 60%; identical coupling graphs do not predict vulnerability, and attacks degrade QRAC success probabilities.
AI.motivation: Quantum processors remain vulnerable to crosstalk-induced effects even as hardware architectures evolve, so the practical security impact of crosstalk-based attacks across real devices needs experimental characterization.
AI.method: Experimental investigation of crosstalk-induced attacks on six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor, measuring victim-qubit measurement outcome-flip probabilities, comparing vulnerability profiles of processors with identical coupling graphs, and evaluating attack impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs).
AI.result: Attacks succeed on all platforms due to persistent crosstalk, though effectiveness varies significantly across devices; outcome-flip probability reaches up to 60%; processors with identical coupling graphs show different vulnerability profiles, and QRAC average success probabilities degrade under attack.
AI.conclusion: Crosstalk-induced attacks are practically relevant across superconducting platforms and cannot be predicted from connectivity alone; QRACs are a concrete application where these attacks cause measurable degradation.

title: Quantum Relative Entropy and Information Flux Resolve Wavefunction Collapse in Spacelike-Separated QED Waveguides
summary: Resolving how first-order quantum coherence and definite measurement outcomes emerge from entangled vacuum fluctuations across spacelike-separated regions is unified here by the principle that quantum relative entropy governs the energy-information flux across causal boundaries [P.~Dorau and A.~Much, Phys.~Rev.~Lett.~\textbf{136}, 091602 (2026)]. We establish the exact quantum-optical realization of this principle using dual, spacelike-separated entangled nonlinear biphoton sources implemented in quantum electrodynamics waveguides pumped by an optical frequency comb and seeded by a continuous-wave laser in a coherent state $|α\rangle$. We demonstrate that single-photon-added coherent states (SPACS) generated via coherent seeding possess a quantum relative entropy that precisely quantifies the entanglement deficit between signal and idler fields. Tracing over the unmeasured idler continuum yields an exact spatial Lindblad master equation along the propagation axis, proving that spatial dephasing is driven by an information divergence flux determined by the SPACS overlap fidelity $F = |α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$. Uniting this relative-entropy flow with quotient measurement theory (detailed in Section~S3 of the Supplemental Material), we rigorously resolve nonlocal wavefunction collapse into local coset projections---explaining macroscopic state reduction without superluminal signaling. This exact open-system framework simultaneously saturates the wave-particle-entanglement triality [T.~H.~Yoon and M.~Cho, Sci.~Adv.~\textbf{7}, eabi9268 (2021)] and anchors hardware-native time--frequency Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill stabilizers to the comb symplectic structure.

AI.tldr: The authors claim an exact quantum-optical realization of a relative-entropy principle governing energy-information flux across causal boundaries, using dual spacelike-separated biphoton sources in QED waveguides. They argue that SPACS accumulated relative entropy quantifies the signal-idler entanglement deficit, derive a spatial Lindblad master equation with dephasing tied to the overlap fidelity F=|α|²/(1+|α|²), and reinterpret nonlocal collapse as local coset projections, while linking the framework to wave-particle-entanglement triality and GKP stabilizers.
AI.motivation: To unify the emergence of first-order quantum coherence and definite measurement outcomes from entangled vacuum fluctuations across spacelike-separated regions, and to explain nonlocal wavefunction collapse (macroscopic state reduction) without superluminal signaling within an exact open-system description.
AI.method: An exact quantum-optical realization of a relative-entropy principle using dual spacelike-separated entangled nonlinear biphoton sources in QED waveguides pumped by an optical frequency comb and coherently seeded (|α⟩). Single-photon-added coherent states (SPACS) serve as the diagnostic; tracing over the unmeasured idler continuum yields a spatial Lindblad master equation along the propagation axis, combined with quotient measurement theory to recast collapse as local coset projections.
AI.result: SPACS generated by coherent seeding possess a quantum relative entropy that precisely quantifies the signal-idler entanglement deficit; spatial dephasing is shown to be driven by an information-divergence flux set by the SPACS overlap fidelity F=|α|²/(1+|α|²); nonlocal collapse is resolved into local coset projections; the framework is claimed to saturate the wave-particle-entanglement triality and to anchor hardware-native time-frequency GKP stabilizers to the comb symplectic structure.
AI.conclusion: Quantum relative entropy is presented as a unifying, exact open-system principle connecting coherence emergence, spatial dephasing, and measurement-outcome definiteness across causal boundaries, with concrete waveguide-comb implementations and compatibility with triality and GKP-stabilizer architectures.

title: From maximum work to maximum power in an optimally controlled quantum Ising Otto engine
summary: In finite-time quantum Otto engines, maximizing power requires balancing the duration of the unitary strokes against the losses from nonadiabatic excitations. We address this trade-off in an Otto engine with a free-fermion working medium, using quantum optimal control. Having determined the single-particle energy scales that maximize ideal work at fixed reservoir temperatures, we realize them as the two endpoint Hamiltonians of a transverse-field Ising chain, connected by a path that crosses the quantum critical point. Optimal control of the unitary strokes yields near-ideal work on a time scale growing linearly with system size, instead of quadratically as for linear driving. We derive a time-rescaling relation that maps protocols with different energy scales onto a single reference problem and, for complete thermalization strokes of fixed duration, use it to build an analytical model of the cycle power. The model predicts two competing maximum-power regimes: a slow branch that approaches the ideal work, and a fast, size-independent branch that trades work for a shorter cycle and dominates above a crossover size, in quantitative agreement with numerical optimal-control results. It also identifies power-optimal energy scales that differ from the work-optimal ones and further increase the power. Our results provide a predictive approach to jointly optimizing the operating conditions and finite-time dynamics of quantum heat engines.

AI.tldr: Quantum optimal control is applied to finite-time Otto engines with a free-fermion (transverse-field Ising chain) working medium to jointly optimize driving protocols and operating conditions, revealing two competing power-maximizing regimes and power-optimal energy scales distinct from work-optimal ones.
AI.motivation: In finite-time quantum Otto engines, maximizing power requires balancing the duration of unitary strokes against losses from nonadiabatic excitations. The paper aims to resolve this trade-off and to jointly optimize operating conditions (energy scales) and finite-time dynamics rather than treating them separately.
AI.method: The authors use quantum optimal control on a free-fermion working medium. They first identify the single-particle energy scales that maximize ideal work at fixed reservoir temperatures, then realize these as the two endpoint Hamiltonians of a transverse-field Ising chain joined by a path crossing the quantum critical point. They derive a time-rescaling relation mapping protocols with different energy scales onto a single reference problem, and use it to construct an analytical model of cycle power for complete thermalization strokes of fixed duration.
AI.result: Optimal control of unitary strokes achieves near-ideal work on a time scale growing linearly with system size, instead of quadratically as with linear driving. The analytical model predicts two competing maximum-power regimes: a slow branch approaching ideal work, and a fast, size-independent branch trading work for a shorter cycle that dominates above a crossover size, in quantitative agreement with numerical optimal-control results. Power-optimal energy scales differ from work-optimal ones and further increase power.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a predictive framework for jointly optimizing the operating conditions and finite-time dynamics of quantum heat engines, with the time-rescaling relation and analytical power model enabling quantitative design of power-optimal finite-time cycles.

title: Approaching quantum limits in sub-Rayleigh resolution using phase modulation optimization
summary: Spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) has made significant progress in incoherent optical imaging and has been implemented through various experimental approaches. Holography-based SPADE is widely used in proof-of-principle experiments because of its low cost, stable optical arrangement, and ease of implementation. However, its low photon utilization severely limits its practical applications. Alternating Fourier transforms and phase modulations can implement unitary optical transformations. Building on this idea, we use backpropagation to optimize the phase profiles of spatial light modulators (SLMs) and thereby design quantum measurements that are efficient in both information and energy. We study centroid--separation estimation for two incoherent point sources, using Fisher information or the estimation errors of an auxiliary neural network estimator as optimization objectives. As the number of SLMs increases, the optimized measurements approach the quantum limits characterized by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound and the information-regret tradeoff relation. With a few SLMs, our method can outperform direct imaging, showing its potential for superresolution imaging.

AI.tldr: The paper designs information- and energy-efficient SPADE-type measurements by backpropagating through alternating SLM phase modulations and Fourier transforms, optimizing phase profiles with Fisher information or a neural-network estimator objective; as the number of SLMs grows, the measurements approach quantum limits (quantum Cramér-Rao bound and information-regret tradeoff), and with few SLMs they already beat direct imaging.
AI.motivation: Holography-based SPADE is popular for incoherent optical imaging proof-of-principle work (low cost, stable setup, easy implementation) but suffers from low photon utilization, which severely limits practical use. There is a need for SPADE implementations that are simultaneously efficient in information and energy.
AI.method: Unitary optical transformations are realized via alternating Fourier transforms and phase modulations. The phase profiles of spatial light modulators (SLMs) are optimized by backpropagation to synthesize quantum measurements. The task studied is centroid–separation estimation of two incoherent point sources; optimization objectives are either the Fisher information or the estimation error of an auxiliary neural-network estimator.
AI.result: As the number of SLMs increases, the optimized measurements converge toward the quantum limits described by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound and the information-regret tradeoff relation. With only a few SLMs, the method outperforms direct imaging.
AI.conclusion: Backpropagation-optimized SLM-based unitary circuits yield information- and energy-efficient SPADE measurements that approach quantum limits with modest hardware and exceed direct imaging with few SLMs, indicating promise for superresolution imaging.

title: Effective Thermodynamics of a Volume-Dependent Qubit
summary: We develop an effective thermodynamics for a qubit whose energy gap depends inversely on a volume-like control parameter, $Δ(V)=Δ_0/V$, where $V$ is a spectral-control coordinate rather than a literal mechanical volume. Starting from the canonical Gibbs state, we derive a complete thermodynamic structure from the Helmholtz potential and its Legendre and stability properties, including the fundamental relation $S(U,V)$, a generalized pressure conjugate to $V$, the equation of state $U=PV$, the first law, and the associated Maxwell relations. Reversible adiabats preserve the Gibbs populations and satisfy $TV=\mathrm{const.}$ and $PV^2=\mathrm{const.}$, corresponding to an effective exponent $γ=2$. The resulting effective Carnot cycle attains the Carnot efficiency, $η_{\mathrm{Carnot}}=1-T_C/T_H$, whereas the Otto cycle yields $η_{\mathrm{Otto}}=1-V_{\min}/V_{\max}$ and remains strictly sub-Carnot at finite work output. We identify the source of Otto irreversibility exactly: entropy is produced entirely during the isochoric thermalizations, and the cycle entropy production quantifies the informational mismatch between the adiabatically transported states and the reservoir-selected Gibbs states through the sum of the corresponding quantum relative entropies. Finally, we show that unitary-generated nonpassivity can act as a nonequilibrium battery, producing an apparent efficiency above Carnot when its preparation cost is omitted. At the same time, complete work accounting restores the thermodynamic bound.

AI.tldr: The authors build a complete equilibrium thermodynamics for a qubit with an energy gap inversely proportional to a spectral-control coordinate, Δ(V)=Δ₀/V, showing that reversible adiabats satisfy TV=const. and PV²=const. (effective exponent γ=2), that the resulting Carnot cycle reaches Carnot efficiency while the Otto cycle stays sub-Carnot, and that Otto irreversibility is exactly quantified by quantum relative entropies accumulated during isochoric thermalizations.
AI.motivation: Qubit-based quantum heat engines often lack a rigorous thermodynamic framework connecting state variables, equations of state, and irreversibility to underlying quantum information measures. The paper aims to place a qubit with a tunable spectral gap on the same footing as a classical working fluid, enabling precise identification of cycle efficiencies and the microscopic origin of irreversibility.
AI.method: Starting from the canonical Gibbs state, the authors derive the Helmholtz potential, its Legendre transforms and stability properties, the fundamental relation S(U,V), a generalized pressure conjugate to V, the equation of state U=PV, the first law, and Maxwell relations. They analyze reversible adiabats (constant Gibbs populations), construct effective Carnot and Otto cycles, and quantify entropy production via quantum relative entropies between adiabatically transported states and reservoir Gibbs states. They also examine unitary-generated nonpassivity as a nonequilibrium battery with and without preparation-cost accounting.
AI.result: Reversible adiabats yield TV=const. and PV²=const. (γ=2). The effective Carnot cycle achieves η_Carnot=1−T_C/T_H, whereas the Otto cycle gives η_Otto=1−V_min/V_max and remains strictly sub-Carnot at finite work output. All Otto entropy production occurs during the isochoric thermalizations and equals the sum of quantum relative entropies measuring the mismatch between transported and Gibbs states. Unitary-generated nonpassivity can appear to exceed Carnot efficiency when preparation cost is neglected, but full work accounting restores the thermodynamic bound.
AI.conclusion: The qubit with Δ(V)=Δ₀/V admits a consistent, closed thermodynamic structure analogous to a classical fluid, with an effective polytropic exponent γ=2. Cycle efficiencies follow directly from this structure, and Otto irreversibility is exactly attributable to isochoric thermalization steps via quantum relative entropy. Apparent Carnot violations from nonpassive states are artifacts of incomplete work accounting, confirming that the second-law bound holds once preparation costs are included.

title: Coupling between molecular exchange qubits
summary: Spin triangles are promising systems for defining and manipulating scalar degrees of freedom, such as chirality, partial spin sums, or combinations between the two. Here we extend this analysis to dimers formed by pairs of spin triangles, coupled by exchange or dipolar interactions. We show that the weak-coupling limit warrants the introduction of an effective two-qubit picture, and derive the expressions of the related Hamiltonians as a function of the underlying physical interaction between the triangles. We benchmark this two-qubit Hamiltonian against the microscopic one, and discuss the observable effects of the inter-triangle coupling on the spin-electric transitions between states with different chiralities or partial-spin sums.

AI.tldr: The authors extend the study of spin triangles as platforms for encoding and controlling scalar degrees of freedom (chirality, partial spin sums, or their combinations) to dimers formed by two exchange- or dipolar-coupled spin triangles. In the weak-coupling regime, they establish an effective two-qubit description and derive the corresponding Hamiltonians in terms of the underlying inter-triangle physical interaction.
AI.motivation: Spin triangles host scalar degrees of freedom such as chirality and partial spin sums that are attractive for defining and manipulating quantum information. Whether these degrees of freedom can be exploited in coupled architectures, specifically dimers of exchange- or dipolar-coupled triangles, has not been established, motivating an analysis of how inter-triangle coupling affects the relevant states.
AI.method: The weak-coupling limit is used to justify an effective two-qubit picture for the dimer. The authors derive the effective Hamiltonians as functions of the underlying physical inter-triangle interaction (exchange or dipolar), benchmark this two-qubit Hamiltonian against the full microscopic Hamiltonian, and analyze observable effects of the inter-triangle coupling on spin-electric transitions between states differing in chirality or partial-spin sums.
AI.result: An effective two-qubit Hamiltonian is obtained and validated against the microscopic model, showing that the weak-coupling regime supports a two-qubit description. The inter-triangle coupling is found to produce observable modifications of the spin-electric transitions between states of different chirality or partial spin sums.
AI.conclusion: Dimers of exchange- or dipolar-coupled spin triangles provide a viable extension of the single-triangle paradigm: in the weak-coupling limit they admit an effective two-qubit description, whose validity is benchmarked against the microscopic model, and whose spin-electric transitions are measurably influenced by the inter-triangle coupling.

title: Exponential mixing time for the Davies dynamics of the quantum random energy model
summary:
We prove exponentially slow thermalization for the quantum random energy model (QREM) under Davies dynamics. The QREM is the $n$-qubit Hamiltonian $H=ΓT+U$, where $U$ assigns independent Gaussian energies with variance equal to the system size to computational-basis configurations and $T$ is the transverse field generated by single-qubit Pauli $X$ operators. Let $β_c=\sqrt{2\log 2}$ be the freezing inverse temperature of the classical random energy model.
