For every inverse temperature $β>β_c$ and every transverse-field strength $0\leqΓ<Γ_c(β)$, where $e^{ββ_c}=2\cosh(βΓ_c(β))$, we show that the mixing time of the dissipative Davies dynamics associated with single-qubit Pauli system--bath couplings grows exponentially with the system size, almost surely; the bound is unchanged if the standard zero-Bohr-frequency dephasing terms are included. The result is uniform over all Davies rates satisfying detailed balance and a polynomial upper bound and does not assume primitivity.
  In the spin-glass phase, the Gibbs weight is carried by a sparse family of deep classical configurations that are separated by an extensive Hamming distance. A localization theorem for the QREM [Manai, Warzel, Comm. Math. Phys. 402, 1259 (2023)] transfers this geometry to the corresponding low-energy quantum eigenstates. Consequently, the Gibbs weight of the intermediate spectral sector is exponentially small, while single-qubit bath operators have exponentially small matrix elements between the two macroscopic sides of the bottleneck. A Davies-specific flux estimate then converts these two facts into an exponential lower bound on the mixing time. This gives a rigorous open-system dynamical manifestation of the frozen, localized low-energy structure of the QREM throughout its equilibrium spin-glass phase below the quantum transition line.

AI.tldr: The paper proves exponentially slow thermalization (mixing time growing exponentially in system size $n$, almost surely) for the quantum random energy model under Davies dynamics, for all inverse temperatures $\beta>\beta_c=\sqrt{2\log 2}$ and transverse fields $0\le\Gamma<\Gamma_c(\beta)$, uniform over all detailed-balance Davies rates with polynomial upper bounds and not assuming primitivity.
AI.motivation: Establish a rigorous open-system dynamical signature of the frozen, localized low-energy structure of the QREM in its spin-glass phase, complementing static spectral/localization results (Manai–Warzel) with a genuine thermalization-time statement for physically motivated dissipative dynamics.
AI.method: Analyze the QREM $H=\Gamma T+U$ (independent Gaussian $U$ on computational basis states, transverse field from Pauli $X$) under Davies dynamics with single-qubit Pauli system–bath couplings. Use the Manai–Warzel eigenstate localization theorem to transfer the sparse, extensively Hamming-separated deep-configuration geometry of the spin-glass phase to low-energy quantum eigenstates; combine exponentially small Gibbs weight of the intermediate spectral sector with exponentially small single-qubit matrix elements across the macroscopic bottleneck, and apply a Davies-specific flux estimate to derive the lower bound; result is robust to adding zero-Bohr-frequency dephasing terms.
AI.result: For every $\beta>\beta_c$ and $0\le\Gamma<\Gamma_c(\beta)$ with $e^{\beta\beta_c}=2\cosh(\beta\Gamma_c(\beta))$, the mixing time of the Davies dynamics grows exponentially with $n$, almost surely. The bound holds uniformly over all Davies rates satisfying detailed balance and a polynomial upper bound, and does not require primitivity; including standard zero-Bohr-frequency dephasing leaves the bound unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The QREM exhibits a rigorous dynamical manifestation of freezing/low-energy localization throughout its equilibrium spin-glass phase below the quantum transition line: thermalization is exponentially slow under Davies dynamics, providing an open-system analogue of the frozen, localized structure established statically.

title: Nonuniform Time-bins for Making Raw QRNG Outputs Uniform
summary: Random numbers play a vital role in scientific simulations and cryptography. Both randomness and security are critical requirements for random number generators (RNGs). However, classical RNGs often rely on mathematical assumptions that can compromise security, while quantum RNGs (QRNGs) face challenges, including non-uniform output due to the lack of specialized single-photon sources. In this work, we propose a QRNG model that generates uniformly distributed random numbers using a standard coherent photon source, without requiring heavy attenuation or post-processing. Although the raw data is theoretically free of bias, post-processing, if any, may be required to suppress any classical noise and device imperfections. The proposed method analytically equalizes the output probabilities under the assumed photon-arrival-time model, potentially reducing the need for heavy attenuation and post-processing to correct binning bias. We evaluate the method using real photon-detection timestamps and compare its statistical performance with conventional uniform time binning using the NIST, Dieharder, and ENT test suites. The results demonstrate improved statistical performance for the proposed binning scheme under the tested conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum random number generator (QRNG) that uses a standard coherent photon source and an analytical equalization of photon-arrival-time bin probabilities to produce uniformly distributed random numbers without heavy attenuation or post-processing, and shows improved statistical performance over conventional uniform time binning.
AI.motivation: Randomness and security are both critical for RNGs, but classical RNGs rest on mathematical assumptions that may be broken, while QRNGs typically suffer from non-uniform output because specialized single-photon sources are unavailable and standard sources need heavy attenuation plus post-processing to correct binning bias.
AI.method: A QRNG model based on a standard coherent photon source without heavy attenuation. The method analytically equalizes output probabilities under an assumed photon-arrival-time model, so that binning bias is removed by design rather than by attenuation or post-processing. Evaluation uses real photon-detection timestamps, comparing the proposed binning scheme against conventional uniform time binning.
AI.result: Statistical testing with the NIST, Dieharder, and ENT suites on real detected timestamps shows improved statistical performance for the proposed equalized binning scheme relative to conventional uniform time binning under the tested conditions. The raw data is theoretically bias-free, though post-processing may still be applied to suppress residual classical noise and device imperfections.
AI.conclusion: Analytical equalization of photon-arrival-time bin probabilities enables a practical QRNG with a standard coherent source that attains uniform output and better statistical quality while potentially reducing the need for heavy attenuation and post-processing.

title: Quantum trajectory of a spin oscillator, continuous retrodiction beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
summary: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation in quantum mechanics limits the precision of predicting the outcome of measurements of any non-commuting observables. However, this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of the outcomes of past measurements. Here, we experimentally demonstrate this using a spin oscillator consisting of $ 5.17 \times 10^{10}$ rubidium atoms. Through weak continuous measurements, we monitor canonical spin observables $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ with $[\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}},\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}] = i\hbar$. By combining information obtained before and after time $t$, we retrodict the outcomes of measurements of $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ at time $t$ with variances that remain, concurrently over 1.4 hours, $\sim$ 1.01 dB below the bound set by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We also infer and demonstrate the ability to retrodict, with the same precision, the measurement outcomes for arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator. This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies.

AI.tldr: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation limits predicting future measurement outcomes of non-commuting observables, but not retrodicting past ones; here the authors experimentally retrodict past spin-oscillator measurement outcomes below the Heisenberg bound using weak continuous monitoring combined with information before and after time t.
AI.motivation: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation constrains the precision of predicting outcomes of non-commuting observables, but this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of past measurement outcomes. The authors aim to experimentally demonstrate this retrodictive advantage beyond the Heisenberg bound.
AI.method: A spin oscillator of 5.17×10^10 rubidium atoms is monitored via weak continuous measurements, tracking canonical spin observables x_A and p_A with [x_A, p_A] = iħ. Information obtained before and after time t is combined to retrodict the outcomes of x_A and p_A measurements at time t.
AI.result: Retrodicted variances remain concurrently ~1.01 dB below the Heisenberg bound over 1.4 hours. The same precision is achieved for retrodicting measurement outcomes of arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator.
AI.conclusion: The experiment demonstrates that retrodiction of past measurement outcomes can surpass the Heisenberg uncertainty bound, with prospects for quantum measurement research and quantum-enhanced sensing combining trajectory and entanglement strategies.

title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls
summary: High-fidelity quantum gates are a central requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet their implementation is limited by the sensitivity of qubits to environmental noise and by control non-idealities. To mitigate these effects, quantum gates can be designed as dynamically corrected gates (DCGs), where control sequences are engineered to suppress the impact of errors on the resulting operation. Many methods in the literature are able to synthesize DCGs, but they typically rely on numerical optimization, with synthesis times on the order of minutes per gate. Here, we propose an automated semi-analytical method that reduces this cost by orders of magnitude, synthesizing smooth, robust control pulses in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness. Our approach is based on the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, where quantum evolution is mapped onto a geometric space curve whose geometric properties determine the target gate and its robustness. We parameterize the curve in the Frenet-Serret frame and employ the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) to design controls that are robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. The PMP is formulated as a boundary-value problem and solved using a shooting method. The Frenet-Serret frame is integrated using Rodrigues' formula. Starting from a reference solution, we gradually vary the target rotation angle to construct a library of solutions, whose interpolation provides initial guesses for the shooting parameters of new target gates. We evaluated the method on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, obtaining a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparation of the interpolation base. Quantum propagation yielded nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.

AI.tldr: An automated semi-analytical SCQC+PMP shooting method synthesizes smooth, robust single-qubit dynamically corrected gates in ~40 ms each (orders of magnitude faster than numerical optimization), achieving infidelities below 1e-9 with verified robustness to amplitude and dephasing errors.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity quantum gates are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation but are limited by qubit sensitivity to environmental noise and control non-idealities. Dynamically corrected gates (DCGs) can suppress these errors, but existing synthesis methods rely on numerical optimization costing on the order of minutes per gate, making large-scale gate library generation impractical.
AI.method: The authors use the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, mapping quantum evolution onto a geometric space curve whose properties encode the target gate and its robustness. The curve is parameterized in the Frenet-Serret frame (integrated via Rodrigues' formula), and the Pontryagin Maximum Principle is formulated as a boundary-value problem solved by a shooting method to design controls robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. A reference solution is used to gradually vary the target rotation angle, building a solution library whose interpolation supplies initial shooting guesses for new target gates.
AI.result: Evaluated on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, the method achieved a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparing the interpolation base. Quantum propagation gave nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors, at fidelity and robustness comparable to numerical optimization.
AI.conclusion: The semi-analytical SCQC/PMP shooting approach automates synthesis of smooth, robust DCGs at orders-of-magnitude lower cost than numerical optimization, enabling fast generation of large gate libraries with excellent nominal fidelity and verified noise robustness for single-qubit rotations.

title: Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
summary: Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.

AI.tldr: QC-AFQMC trial states are distilled from matchgate-shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware autoregressive transformer NQS, enabling overlap/local-energy evaluation without repeated shadow averaging and cutting classical cost by ~99% while recovering accurate reaction energies.
AI.motivation: In QC-AFQMC, the quantum trial state is represented by matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots; this classical post-processing is a computational bottleneck. In addition, hardware noise degrades standard QC-AFQMC accuracy.
AI.method: Distill matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). The NQS serves as the AFQMC trial state, evaluating overlaps, force biases, and local energies directly without repeatedly summing over shadows. Shadow data are used only for training.
AI.result: For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-aware NQS recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, whereas standard QC-AFQMC with the same shadow data gives qualitatively inaccurate results due to hardware noise. Estimated classical cost drops ~99% versus the prior QC-AFQMC implementation.
AI.conclusion: Distilling matchgate shadows into a noise-aware autoregressive NQS trial state mitigates hardware noise and removes the shadow-summation bottleneck, yielding accurate reaction energetics at a ~99% reduction in classical cost.

title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
summary: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

AI.tldr: Compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that supply wavefunction overlaps accelerates hybrid quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, achieving chemically accurate simulations up to 40 qubits on Google's Willow processor.
AI.motivation: Strongly correlated electron simulation is a central quantum-computing goal. Hybrid approaches that use a quantum processor to prepare trial wavefunctions for classical QMC are promising, but repeatedly processing quantum measurements is computationally prohibitive, limiting practical scalability.
AI.method: The authors compress quantum measurement data into machine-learning surrogate models that efficiently return the wavefunction overlaps required by QMC. This replaces costly repeated post-processing of shot data with fast model inference on the classical coprocessor, creating an accelerated quantum-classical QMC loop.
AI.result: Order-of-magnitude (orders of magnitude) acceleration of quantum-classical QMC, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits—more than doubling the scale of prior hardware demonstrations at comparable accuracy. Demonstrated on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor.
AI.conclusion: Efficient classical reuse of quantum-state information via ML surrogates resolves a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms—one expected to persist into the fault-tolerant era—substantially extending the reach of quantum-assisted strongly correlated simulations.

title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
summary: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors generalize the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) to non-unitary dynamics, compute it for a Haar-random brickwork qudit circuit with local projective measurements, and show that the infinite-temperature ensemble-averaged OTOC decays exponentially at a measurement-rate-dependent rate, forming a causal scrambling front whose bulk signal decays (unlike the unitary case). They validate the predictions with a Monte Carlo framework, direct quantum simulation, and experiments on a trapped-ion quantum computer.
AI.motivation: The OTOC is a standard probe of quantum chaos and information scrambling, but it is defined for unitary evolution. Real devices suffer non-unitary channels (e.g., measurement, noise), so a principled, analytically tractable generalization of the OTOC to non-unitary dynamics is needed to characterize how local non-unitary channels affect many-body scrambling and to benchmark hardware noise.
AI.method: The authors define a generalized OTOC for non-unitary systems and compute the infinite-temperature ensemble-averaged OTOC for a Haar-random brickwork qudit circuit interspersed with local projective measurements. They use transfer-matrix machinery to obtain the asymptotic decay, develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC, and estimate it via direct quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer.
AI.result: The OTOC decays asymptotically exponentially, with a decay rate depending on the measurement rate; in the thermodynamic limit with sparse measurement it is approximately Gaussian. Phenomenologically, a causal scrambling front develops in which, unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. These unitary and non-unitary OTOC signatures are resolved in quantum simulation and on the trapped-ion hardware despite hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: The analytic results characterize how local non-unitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics, and the phenomenology is experimentally accessible on current quantum processors.

title: Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between $\mathsf{StoqMA}$ and $\mathsf{MA}$
summary:
Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain $\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}$, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation $$\mathsf{MA} \subsetneq \mathsf{StoqMA}$$ relative to a classical oracle. The class $\mathsf{StoqMA}$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians.
  Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).

AI.tldr: A classical oracle separates MA from StoqMA, showing that a single Hadamard-basis measurement on a classical reversible circuit (StoqMA) already exceeds every classical verifier, via a Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue / ground-energy estimation problem on sparse high-girth graphs.
AI.motivation: Prior oracle separations along MA ⊆ QCMA ⊆ QMA (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) rely on substantial coherent quantum computation such as the quantum Fourier transform. The paper asks whether a minimal quantum resource suffices to beat all classical verifiers, and identifies StoqMA — a class linked to stoquastic (sign-problem-free) Hamiltonians — as the natural candidate.
AI.method: Constructs a classical oracle problem: given a sparse high-girth graph via adjacency-list oracle, decide whether it has a large or small Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue, i.e., ground-energy estimation for an associated stoquastic Hamiltonian. A StoqMA protocol (classical reversible computation plus one Hadamard-basis measurement) solves it, while no MA verifier can. The construction extends graph-exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).
AI.result: Establishes MA ⊊ StoqMA relative to a classical oracle, the first separation achieved with minimal quantum resources. This complements and strengthens the MA/QCMA/QMA chain, and shows that even sign-problem-free stoquastic Hamiltonian ground-energy estimation can yield oracle separation from classical proof systems.
AI.conclusion: A single Hadamard-basis measurement on a classical reversible circuit already provides strictly more power than any classical verifier, so minimal quantum coherence suffices for super-classical proof verification. This ties the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians to oracle separations and extends the line of graph-exploration speedups to a new separating problem.

title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
summary:
Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity.
  This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy

AI.tldr: QDIFF is a differential testing approach for quantum software stacks that generates input programs via semantics-preserving source-to-source transformations, filters out circuits unsuitable for hardware execution based on static circuit characteristics, and uses distribution comparison functions for extensible equivalence checking.
AI.motivation: Quantum software stacks (QSS) — comprising a quantum programming language, optimizing compiler, simulator, and hardware controller — are advancing rapidly with hardware but are difficult to test due to the probabilistic nature of execution results, absence of clear hardware specifications, and the complexity of quantum programming. Traditional compiler and architecture-simulator testing techniques do not transfer well to this setting.
AI.method: The paper proposes QDIFF, a differential testing approach with three innovations: (1) input programs are generated through semantics-preserving source-to-source transformation to explore program variants; (2) differential testing is accelerated by filtering out quantum circuits not worthwhile to execute on hardware, using static characteristics such as circuit depth, two-qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time; (3) an extensible equivalence-checking mechanism is designed based on distribution comparison functions, including the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and cross-entropy.
AI.result: The abstract does not report quantitative results. The stated outcome is a novel differential testing methodology, QDIFF, that addresses QSS testing challenges through variant generation, static-characteristic-based circuit filtering, and distribution-based equivalence checking.
AI.conclusion: QDIFF provides a principled differential testing framework tailored to quantum software stacks, mitigating probabilistic nondeterminism and hardware cost via semantics-preserving transformations, informed circuit pruning, and extensible statistical equivalence checking.

title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
summary: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.

AI.tldr: Optimal trade-offs in certifying GHZ-class states and reading out the three-tangle from multiple copies of unknown three-qubit pure states are characterized, with exact success probabilities given for four, five, and six copies.
AI.motivation: To quantify the best achievable performance when jointly certifying the GHZ class, extracting a binary three-tangle readout, and retaining quantum state from limited copies of an unknown three-qubit pure state.
AI.method: Uses the vanishing ideal of the null class to define the optimal certification subspace and a polynomial multiplication operator to set the spectral limit for binary readout; a symmetry-based additional-copy theorem derives gains from extra copies. Local Schur measurements and conditional LOCC attain the bounds.
AI.result: Four copies are required for a nonzero certificate; a fifth raises optimal success probability from τ²/48 to 5τ²/72 while retaining the original state; at six copies the optimal certification probability is (39+2S)τ²/296 (S=Σ_X Tr ρ_X²) versus largest exact binary probability τ²/8. A full six-copy branch-record weighted estimator has lower variance than binary thinning.
AI.conclusion: Exact, symmetry-derived bounds link certification success, three-tangle readout, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost, with explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons.

title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description
summary: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.

AI.tldr: A converged open-system model computes level-resolved transmon populations after dispersive readout, predicting persistent bare-level occupations (p2≈1.0×10⁻³, p3≈4.1×10⁻⁵ at n=80) that survive drive-off waits, and benchmark tests show the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates full charge-operator populations (p2 ratio 0.905, p3 ratio 0.759) at switch-off.
AI.motivation: Dispersive readout leaves residual transmon population that can corrupt subsequent operations, but quantitatively converged, level-resolved predictions and a clear assessment of where common approximations (RWA drive, bath models) lose reliability are lacking.
AI.method: Open-system model with RWA for drive and qubit-cavity coupling, quantized cavity mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. Analysis includes drive-off wait dynamics, channel-removal and bath-model controls, and dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks comparing nearest-neighbour RWA drive against the full charge-operator drive. A beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators is tested against a zero-drive ground-state check, and a dressed-basis (secular) construction is introduced.
AI.result: At readout occupation 80: p2 = 1.02×10⁻³, p3 = 4.10×10⁻⁵ persisting after readout; over a 73 ns drive-off wait each level decays <3% at its own relaxation rate (unlike the ~2× drop in residual cavity photons), identifying bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel/bath controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3+ mainly to relaxation, invariant across bath models though absolute values vary up to 15%. title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
summary: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.

title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
comment: 73 pages (18 pages main text, 55 pages Supplementary Information), 8 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/Fanerst/tropidist
summary: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.

AI.tldr: The paper expresses code and circuit distances as tropical partition functions and evaluates them via rank-based dynamic programming with weight-bounded search, achieving exact, certified distances that outperform other exact solvers and expose overestimated distances in prior literature.
AI.motivation: Many published code and circuit distances are only heuristic upper bounds, which undermines code comparisons, schedule choices, and resource estimates. Accurate, certified distances are needed to guide practical design decisions.
AI.method: Both distances are cast as tropical partition functions and computed using rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problem, while proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values.

It certifies distances for codes up to 31,200 qubits (e.g., modular hyperbolic codes) and memory circuits up to 8x10^5 fault mechanisms (e.g., high-rate Cornucopia codes). title: Entropic measures of quantum information
comment: 84-page review article. Comments and suggestions very welcome
summary: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.

AI.tldr: A structured review of quantum entropic information measures—including Rényi and smooth entropies—their principled definitions, interrelations, and applications across quantum communication, cryptography, resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
AI.motivation: Entropy's historical evolution from Clausius (physics) to Shannon (information theory) has produced a productive interplay between the two fields, revealing that no single entropy notion captures all relevant properties of physical systems; hence a diversity of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses, must be considered. The paper motivates a unified, structured overview of these measures.
AI.method: A structured review that systematically characterizes entropies, deriving their definitions from natural physical principles, and surveys a comprehensive array of quantum information measures—including Rényi and smooth entropies—together with their interrelations.
AI.result: The review provides a systematic characterization linking entropy definitions to physical principles, catalogs a comprehensive set of information measures (Rényi, smooth, and related entropies) with their interrelations, and surveys their applications spanning quantum communication, cryptography, resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
AI.conclusion: No single notion of entropy suffices for all physical purposes; a pluralistic family of quantum entropic measures, grounded in physical principles and interconnected, is essential and fruitful for advancing both information theory and physics.

title: Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Lie groups, Schur-Weyl duality and symmetry breaking
summary: We present a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries, and show that the Schur-Weyl duality arises naturally as a realization of this construction with open boundary conditions. Restricting to compact Lie group symmetries, we construct dual models for one-dimensional quantum lattice models exhibiting those symmetries. We demonstrate that matrix product operators enable the explicit construction of intertwiners between the dual theories and their (non-invertible) symmetries. With closed boundary conditions, we can relate the full spectrum of these dual theories by considering all possible twisted boundary conditions.We illustrate how the Peter-Weyl transform appears when the duality acts on the boundary Hilbert space of a $G$-symmetric model. The presented framework generalizes previous work on dualities for unitary fusion category symmetric models. It exemplifies how dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries rely on the relation between a bond algebra and a representation of the symmetry in the lattice as double centralizers. We argue that dual non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking is the mechanism that underlies symmetric tensor network algorithms. We illustrate these results for $U(1)$- and $SU(2)$-symmetric quantum lattice models.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries on 1D quantum lattice models, showing Schur-Weyl duality emerges as a special case with open boundaries and that dualities for finite and continuous symmetries both rest on double-centralizer (bond algebra vs. symmetry representation) relations.
AI.motivation: Previous dualities for unitary fusion category (finite, non-invertible) symmetric lattice models lack a unified treatment that covers continuous (compact Lie group) symmetries. The authors aim to place Schur-Weyl duality, Peter-Weyl theory, and tensor-network algorithms within one common gauging framework.
AI.method: Gauging of continuous symmetries via a bond-algebra/representation double-centralizer structure; construction of dual models for 1D models with compact Lie group symmetries; explicit intertwiners between dual theories and their non-invertible symmetries built with matrix product operators (MPOs); closed boundary conditions handled by summing over all twisted boundary conditions to relate full spectra; Peter-Weyl transform derived on the boundary Hilbert space.
AI.result: Schur-Weyl duality is recovered as the open-boundary realization of the construction; MPOs yield explicit intertwiners; twisted boundary conditions relate the complete spectra of dual theories; the Peter-Weyl transform appears naturally on the boundary Hilbert space of G-symmetric models; the framework generalizes prior unitary-fusion-category dualities. Illustrated for U(1)- and SU(2)-symmetric quantum lattice models.
AI.conclusion: Dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries are unified as relations between a bond algebra and a lattice symmetry representation acting as double centralizers. Non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking in the dual describes the mechanism behind symmetric tensor-network algorithms, providing a common language for fusion-category and Lie-group dualities.

title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
comment: Accepted manuscript for publication in Frontiers in Communications and Networks . This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n.101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the Quantum Internet should not only transport quantum states and distribute entanglement but should exploit quantum phenomena directly in realizing network functionalities, proposing entanglement as a stateful resource, two quantum-native mechanisms as proof points, and Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction.
AI.motivation: The prevailing view of the Quantum Internet confines quantum phenomena to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded in classical abstractions. This is necessary but incomplete, and the authors seek a broader architectural thesis.
AI.method: A perspective/position argument: (1) establishes entanglement as a stateful network resource that is non-locally distributed, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades via decoherence, requiring its state to be visible to functionalities acting on it; (2) uses two mechanisms as proof points of a quantum-native functional design space—entanglement generation during propagation via coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that departs from the physical graph; (3) identifies Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction complementing classical addressing and signaling.
AI.result: The examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement rather than by physical connectivity alone.
AI.conclusion: The perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2610.19779
summary: Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

AI.tldr: Exhaustive enumeration shows that process tomography with a fixed measurement basis can be done with 0, 1, or 5 single-qubit Pauli gates for n = 3, 5, 7 qubits, versus 6, 10, 14 for first-order and 6, 50, 308 for full minimum-weight decoding.
AI.motivation: Decoder design in stabilizer-code-based process tomography is nearly always fixed to the standard minimum-weight decoder, so the physical gate cost of the recovery is treated as bookkeeping rather than as a resource. With a fixed measurement basis that cost becomes a genuine resource, and the minimal number of physical single-qubit Pauli gates needed is unknown.
AI.method: Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery (decoder) design for n = 3, 5 and 7 qubits under a fixed measurement basis, with channel rank determined by exact modular arithmetic at two primes.
AI.result: Minimal gate counts are 0, 1 and 5 for n = 3, 5, 7, versus 6, 10, 14 for first-order decoding and 6, 50, 308 for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on the number of corrected sites, not their identity, separating the two halves of the design problem. More correction is not monotonically better: at n = 7 full decoding loses three rank dimensions, and with a calibration-residual floor the n = 3 precision curve is U-shaped. The three-gate design exceeds the standard six-gate decoder by 9.5x at the median of 40 sampled working points and by 1.8x to 88x at every one. A 10 mrad rms error costs 1.2e7 shots in 65 s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point; n >= 5 is limited by conditioning, not gate count. Optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they split the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by 1.3e-3 while keeping the Jacobian at full rank.
AI.conclusion: Decoder gate count is a genuine, enumerable resource that can be minimized far below standard minimum-weight decoding, and the precision ordering advantage over the standard decoder is working-point independent even though its magnitude is not.

title: Testing Gravitationally-Induced-Entanglement with Massive Particles and Quantum Clocks
summary: We present an experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a levitated particle with an array of quantum clocks. By harnessing the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, our scheme offers a conceivable path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks in the laboratory. Crucially, this setup will probe a genuinely relativistic effect one that requires the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass and cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses. Therefore, observing this entanglement would provide evidence for the quantised nature of active gravitational mass -- which has not been tested in any prior experiment -- rather than for spatial coherence of fixed masses,which is routinely tested in matterwave interferometers

AI.tldr: An experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a micrometer-scale levitated particle with an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, probing a genuinely relativistic effect tied to the quantised nature of active gravitational mass.
AI.motivation: Prior gravity-induced entanglement schemes test spatial coherence of fixed masses (routinely probed in matterwave interferometers), rather than whether the internal clock energy contributing to active gravitational mass is quantised. No prior experiment has tested the quantised nature of active gravitational mass.
AI.method: Propose exploiting the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale levitated particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, engineering a gravitationally mediated entanglement between the levitated particle and the clock array that relies on the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass.
AI.result: The scheme offers a conceivable laboratory path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks, isolating a relativistic effect that cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses.
AI.conclusion: Observing the predicted entanglement would provide evidence for the quantised nature of active gravitational mass rather than for spatial coherence of fixed masses, marking a qualitatively new test of quantum gravity.

title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
summary: Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.

AI.tldr: This work maps the Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) landscape for Site-2 $^{167}$Er$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ using a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian with anisotropic field covariance from the native $^{89}$Y lattice, yielding a Pareto-optimal frontier balancing Y-bath pure-dephasing lifetimes against microwave control authority.
AI.motivation: Erbium-doped solids are promising for quantum-network memories, but their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at ZEFOZ points can mitigate this decoherence, motivating a systematic evaluation of the available operating landscape.
AI.method: The ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}$Er$^{3+}$ is evaluated by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment together with an anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived directly from the native $^{89}$Y crystal lattice. Operating-point screening criteria are applied to construct a Pareto-optimal frontier over four transition pairs, trading Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T^{(2)}_{\phi,Y}$) against microwave control authority. A Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis tests robustness of the operating coordinates.

Uncompensated Hamiltonian deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition off its nominal field, but shifted operating points are recoverable via numerical vector-field recalibration; Pareto-optimal coordinates were recovered for all sampled perturbations, with $84.1^{\text{st}}$-percentile field relocations of 10.95–27.97 mT.
AI.conclusion: ZEFOZ operation offers a route to long pure-dephasing lifetimes with usable microwave control, and the Pareto-optimal operating points are robust to Hamiltonian uncertainty when recalibrated. Reported lifetimes are conditional on the temporal-correlation model, and operation near 10 mK is required to suppress Er-induced spectral diffusion via electronic-spin polarization.

title: Quantum enhanced beam displacement estimation: sensitivity limits, optimal probes, and measurement schemes
summary: We investigate the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements and identify optimal strategies that attain them, using the framework of mode parameter estimation. We contrast two families of states with different resource constraints, using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. First, for fixed total photon number states, the optimal state is identified and we show that it asymptotically approaches a rotated NOON state. The sensitivity bound is compared to that of an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state with fixed average photon number. Finally, we propose concrete measurement schemes using the method of moments and show that the twin-Fock state may provide a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this task. Our work provides a broader benchmark for developing practical strategies for spatial sensing at the quantum limit.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements within the framework of mode parameter estimation, comparing Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs under fixed total photon number versus fixed average photon number constraints, and proposing practical measurement schemes.
AI.motivation: Small transverse beam displacements are a key target for quantum-enhanced spatial sensing, but a unified benchmark of the fundamental sensitivity limits across different resource constraints and mode bases was lacking. The work aims to identify optimal states and strategies that actually attain these limits.
AI.method: The problem is cast as mode parameter estimation using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. Two families of states are contrasted under different resource constraints: (i) fixed total photon number, for which the optimal state is derived and shown to asymptotically approach a rotated NOON state; (ii) fixed average photon number, compared against an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state. Concrete measurement schemes are proposed via the method of moments.
AI.result: For fixed total photon number, the optimal state is identified and shown to asymptotically approach a rotated NOON state; its sensitivity bound is benchmarked against the asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state at fixed mean photon number. Using method-of-moments measurements, the twin-Fock state is shown to offer a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this displacement-sensing task.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a broader benchmark for practical spatial-sensing strategies at the quantum limit, clarifying which states and measurements are optimal under given resource constraints and highlighting twin-Fock states as a practical substitute for rotated NOON states.

title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
summary: Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

AI.tldr: DiffSequence-Q is a hybrid multinomial diffusion model that generates protein sequences conditioned on per-residue secondary structure and a continuous solubility target, using quantum auxiliary supervision during training while generating sequences purely by classical reverse diffusion.
AI.motivation: Designing protein sequences that simultaneously satisfy secondary structure requirements and solubility targets is difficult; the authors aim to combine structure- and solubility-conditioned generation with quantum auxiliary supervision to improve sequence quality and solubility.
AI.method: A hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on per-residue secondary structure and a continuous solubility target. During training, a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) serves as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations; its auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to shape the denoising model. At inference, sequences are generated entirely via classical reverse diffusion.
AI.result: On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Using a separately trained solubility predictor, the best QNN and QKAN configurations yielded mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the MLP baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization showed biological activity across three protein families: selected defensins strongly inhibited Aspergillus niger, and xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases showed substantial enzymatic activity.
AI.conclusion: DiffSequence-Q provides a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with quantum auxiliary supervision improving predicted solubility and experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
summary: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.

AI.tldr: Under thermal and pure loss, noisy boson and fermion sampling can be classically simulated in polynomial time for any fixed nonzero loss rate (with high probability over Haar-random interferometers), and quasipolynomially under a flatness assumption without Haar randomness.
AI.motivation: Sampling experiments are leading candidates for demonstrating quantum computational advantage, but their robustness to experimental noise (such as photon loss) is not fully understood. The authors aim to establish when loss renders these sampling tasks classically simulable.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss (including pure loss). They analyze Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, using Haar-random interferometers and a "flatness" assumption on the ideal output distribution.
AI.result: For all three settings, they obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption yields quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant per-layer thermal loss, the flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Fock-state results cover dilute and saturated regimes and strengthen near full input filling: with only a bounded number of empty input modes, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges to an interferometer-independent distribution as the number of modes grows.
AI.conclusion: Loss substantially weakens the hardness of boson and fermion sampling: at any fixed nonzero loss rate these tasks become classically simulable, with convergence to interferometer-independent behavior in the near-full-filling regime.

title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
summary: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
summary: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
summary: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.
